#4896. When the Mountain Follows You Home: What Recovery Looks Like for Outdoor Accident Survivors

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

How a new wave of mental health professionals is helping people confront the trauma that can linger long after they make it back.

ON A LATE fall day in 2023, Laura Stilwell and her boyfriend, Marcus Wybrow, were descending the long mountain trail back to their vehicle after a day of ice-climbing among the rugged peaks west of Calgary, Alberta.

Wybrow, 29, was close to reaching full certification as an alpine guide. Stilwell, 27, had some backcountry experience, but this was her first time ice-climbing. They hadn’t attempted anything most climbers would consider difficult or risky. The point was simply to be in the mountains together, and for Wybrow to introduce Stilwell to a sport he loved.

Avalanche Canada, the main organization issuing the public avalanche forecasts that backcountry enthusiasts check before heading out, wasn’t yet forecasting for the season. (It was too early in the season to warrant forecasts.) Though there wasn’t much snow along the couple’s route, the pair carried avalanche gear to be safe.”

Then, as they hiked toward the trailhead, the snow suddenly cracked off the slope above and slid fast, overwhelming them in white chaos. The avalanche mostly buried Stilwell and fully engulfed Wybrow. It threw Stilwell onto her left side; her right hand was the only part of her body that remained unburied. With that hand, she was able to clear the snow from her face so she could breathe—then started digging herself out, screaming. She isn’t sure how long it took to free herself, but it felt like an eternity.

But this story isn’t about that horrific day. It’s about what happens after.

MANY SURVIVORS OF accidents—climbing falls, near drownings, mountain bike crashes, exposure, even near misses while hiking or trail running—suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Other mental and emotional injuries unique to outdoor accidents abound in these individuals too, including loss of identity and a severed connection to the natural world that once brought feelings of awe and peace. That’s all on top of anxiety, depression, and grief.

Yet we often don’t hear about this terrible aftermath, or how those suffering might find a way through it.

That’s because most narratives about adventure sport accidents tend to deal with the incident itself—the factors, both human and natural, that led up to it, and what it took to survive—while shying away from the psychological impact on those involved.

This is partly due to a culture at large that struggles to deal with mental health issues in general, combined with an outdoor one that has historically prized independence, stoicism, and strength. “Many of us learned how to disconnect from ourselves in order to respond to an emergency, but very few of us were ever taught how to reconnect once the emergency was over,” says Jenny Fiebig, a licensed clinical professional counselor and one of the first therapists to specialize in outdoor trauma.

At the same time, shockingly little access to mental health resources exists in the small mountain towns that are the hubs for these sports—despite the fact many of these areas have exploded in population since the pandemic, as has participation in the activities.

Climbing, ski touring, surfing, kayaking, and trail running are all among the fastest-growing sports in the country. But while many therapists are well trained in trauma, says Fiebig, they’re not always trained in outdoor culture. “If someone doesn’t understand why a person would willingly return to a landscape where they experienced trauma, or put themselves out there in the first place, it’s easy to misinterpret that decision as avoidance, denial, or unnecessary risk.”

The result is that those struggling with this complex trauma have had almost nowhere to turn, leaving a rapidly increasing subset of people isolated in silence. Until now.

Passionate recreationalists and mental health professionals are beginning to address that gap and offer alternative modalities to help outdoor accident survivors heal and to support victims’ families and communities as well. Some of these modalities are new, like peer-support groups and somatic nervous system exercises that help survivors reconnect with nature as part of the healing process. Others, like one-on-one talk therapy, are not revolutionary, but they’ve been dramatically underused for healing in a community that so desperately needs it.

Previously, the response to trauma in mountain towns was largely along the lines of “Let’s go drink a beer and forget about it,” says Fiebig, who works with Colorado-based Survivors of Outdoor Adventures and Recovery (SOAR), one of the organizations leading this movement that has nationwide reach and is growing. “Ignoring the signs or symptoms of PTSD affects relationships, jobs, marriages. It becomes systemic. There’s a high suicide rate in mountain towns, a high depression rate—mental health is a huge issue.”

In adventure culture, “we weren’t supposed to talk about our traumas,” says Darcy Chenoweth, DNP, a 49-year-old psychiatric nurse practitioner in Missoula, Montana, who’s also a mountaineer, climber, and skier. Chenoweth is on the board of directors for Canmore, Alberta–based Mountain Muskox, another leading organization in the field, for which she coauthored a paper on care approaches to trauma and loss in the mountains.

Once, when Chenoweth was talking through her own outdoor trauma with a friend with whom she ice-climbed, he told her she “was just being highly sensitive.”

This new movement is different from anything that came before because most of the professionals involved have been through outdoor trauma themselves, and they’ve seen firsthand how the care gap leaves survivors adrift in the hellish experiences that come after disaster. Also, given that adventure sports and the outdoor arena have historically been male-dominated—and traditionally masculine traits like speed, capability, and infallible expertise have been valued, while showing vulnerability was often seen as weakness—perhaps it’s no surprise that this movement is almost entirely women-led.

And for Laura Stilwell, it couldn’t have come soon enough.

AFTER THAT DAY in the mountains, Stilwell descended into a nightmare of grief tangled up with trauma, an emotional storm that many adventure accident survivors experience. She couldn’t sleep. When she woke in the predawn, she’d think, It’s too early, I can’t make it through a day this long. In the immediate aftermath, she was “a numb ghost, feeling nothing, not really living,” she says.

Then the pain roared in. Anything that sparked a memory of Wybrow, from books to clothing to photos, sent her into a sudden breakdown. Sometimes her grief wailed louder, the trauma manifesting in nightmares and hypervigilance. She’d lived in Squamish, British Columbia, for only a year at that point; her community was still fairly small and couldn’t identify with what she was going through.

Most of her friends were newer to adventure sports, “without a grasp of how bad things can be,” she says. “I was in that camp too, and then this happened to me, and it’s like that innocence just gets ripped away.”

Stilwell also grappled with thoughts of what she could have done differently that day, and battled with blame, shame, and guilt—another unique layer of trauma that outdoor accident survivors frequently suffer.

Many of these activities require an enormous amount of knowledge and skill, from snow science or river hydraulics to understanding weather, navigating remote terrain, operating technical equipment, performing companion rescue, and accepting inherent risk. An accident is often treated as a gap in that knowledge—a mistake of sometimes fatal proportions for which judgment, both from the self and others, is often lobbed liberally.

Consider, for example, the judgment-laden media coverage of the February 2026 avalanche near Lake Tahoe in Northern California that claimed nine lives, six of them mothers.

“Folks who choose to connect to outdoor spaces through recreation often experience a joy and connection that is hard to find in our manufactured way of life,” says Fiebig. “But when we put ourselves in the ‘risk’ of being outside, we also get shamed when things go wrong—a sort of ‘well, why did you choose to be there?’”

Chenoweth says that the rise of social media, in addition to glorifying adventure without acknowledging the social and emotional costs, only exacerbates the situation. These platforms allow “many people outside the community [to] live vicariously through the activities of mountain athletes. This often leads to outside judgment from those with no knowledge of the individuals involved in an incident or its context,” she writes in her coauthored paper.

The adventure community itself can also contribute to the shame survivors feel by scrutinizing the accident for mistakes. This is partly to learn from the incident, and partly a defense tactic to distance ourselves from the trauma.

“There’s a culture of analyzing all the data after an accident that takes the humanity out of the survivors,” says Fiebig. This scrutiny, she says, may send survivors into a “shame spiral.” “We need to know what happened, but we also need to make that space for the survivor to feel cared for, to feel validated that they did the best they could do, and recognize the pain that they just went through.”

Trying to navigate her own mental health, Stilwell did one-on-one therapy. It was a lifeline, but when a session would end, she’d panic knowing that she had to get through an entire week before the next session. She’d been a digital marketer, but she couldn’t work. She couldn’t focus, engage with other people, or regulate her emotions enough for a professional setting. She started watching television for up to 10 hours a day as a survival mechanism to distract herself from the pain, even while contemplating not being alive anymore at all.

SOME MAY STILL question why anyone would venture into the outdoors knowing that these pursuits might deliver such trauma and loss.

Science offers answers. Even just 20 minutes per day spent in nature can lower stress hormone levels, boost mental health, and increase life expectancy, and spending time outdoors provides an added sense of well-being specifically for women, per research. Time in nature serves as an escape from the everyday pressures unique to females (such as conforming to expectations about weight, appearance, and demeanor), according to an REI study on women in the outdoors.

But many recreationalists say it’s about more than what the research shows. The very presence of risk is part of what makes adventure so alluring and often so hard to describe to those outside of the community. Navigating situations with risk, where individual decisions, grit, and capability can determine personal fate, demands the kind of complete focus that some try to achieve through meditation practice—and is often impossible to find in our busy world.

Navigating those situations in the company of others can also be a profound experience. “I have built the strongest, deepest, most fulfilling relationships in my life while doing activities like climbing or ski touring,” Stilwell says. “You put yourself in a situation where there’s some risk involved, [along with] decision-making and fear, you have to manage your nervous system—it allows you to connect with somebody so much deeper, to get to know what motivates them, what scares them, what exhilarates them. And I feel so much more seen in those environments.”

Then there’s the awe factor. Awe, “our response to powerful things that are obscure, vast, and mysterious,” can have benefits from “calming inflammation to activating the vagus nerve, deactivating our brain’s stress center, to reducing pain perception,” according to Dacher Keltner, PhD, author of Awe: The New Science of Everyday Wonder and How It Can Transform Your Life. Awe often helps us transcend the self so that even our perception of time changes and we feel part of something bigger. Many people who love the outdoors will say, in one way or another, that connecting to this feeling through recreation might be the closest they come to grace.

But, says Chenoweth, “awe and tragedy are not separate. Both push us beyond ourselves, where the ideas we have about the world shift, and sometimes shatter, and human consciousness confronts the unknown. You can’t say, ‘I’ll choose awe, and avoid tragedy.’ The unknown holds both.”

STILWELL’S THERAPIST EVENTUALLY recommended that she check out SOAR.

Starr Jamison, an outdoor professional in Telluride, Colorado, founded SOAR after losing three friends to separate avalanches in a single year and wading through her own grief and traumatic experiences. She also watched people involved in or adjacent to accidents attempt or commit suicide after losing loved ones—including after a highly publicized avalanche in October 2017 on Montana’s Imp Peak that claimed the life of 23-year-old Inge Perkins, a rising star in the backcountry skiing and climbing worlds.

Perkins’s partner and famed climber Hayden Kennedy, 27, survived the slide but couldn’t locate Perkins, who was buried with her transceiver turned off. After searching in vain for hours, Kennedy drove home to their apartment in Bozeman, wrote a note describing where to search for her body, and then took his own life.

That tragedy spurred a reeling mountain community to reckon with unaddressed trauma. Organizations formed to support the professional community of guides, ski patrollers, wildland firefighters, and others who are outdoors for their jobs, including Responder Alliance, run by Laura McGladrey, and Climbing Grief Fund, started by Madaleine Sorkin.

But Jamison found that support for people who simply wanted to adventure for the love of it (rather than it being their job) remained nonexistent. Eventually she was connected to a couple of mental health professionals who were also considering how to bridge this gap, including Fiebig. SOAR piloted its first peer-support group for outdoor trauma survivors in 2021.

The organization now offers community connection workshops on topics such as mindfulness, survivor’s guilt, and neuroplastic healing. It also maintains a growing public list of counselors, therapists, body workers, psychiatric nurse practitioners, and resiliency coaches who speak the language of outdoor trauma and grief.

SOAR’s peer-support model is akin to Alcoholics Anonymous, but whereas AA is led by rotating members, these groups are led by professional facilitators. The sessions, which run monthly for five to six months, are free and often take place over Zoom, so they can be as accessible as possible. SOAR’s groups comprise people with common experiences: those who survived an outdoor incident in which another person perished; those who’ve lost a partner but weren’t on the scene; parents who’ve lost children to outdoor trauma; people who’ve sustained injuries in adventures; and others. Stilwell joined a group facilitated by Fiebig specifically for survivors of outdoor accidents in which their partners had died.

Like most of the women leading this movement, Fiebig, 46, follows the wounded healer arc (essentially, helping others as a means of healing yourself). She’s a whitewater boater who experienced several near misses with drowning in her 20s, and she once fell into a Class 5 stretch of river without a life jacket when the bank gave way while she was hiking. She chalked it up to not having enough skills and dismissed the accompanying emotional trauma as invalid, because, after all, she’d survived. It’s a common response, but insidiously dangerous. While not glaringly tragic, such experiences can have serious psychological impacts—and more so when they’re cumulative.

“I never sought help because of the shame of the experience—I felt like I could have prevented it,” Fiebig says. “Especially as a woman in the outdoors, it was easy for me to immediately go to blaming myself for not being good enough.”

Fiebig still grieves the two decades of her life during which she believed she was “not enough” because of what she perceived to be her mistakes, which made her pull back from whitewater even though she loved it. “I want to help marginalized communities work through their traumas so they’re not missing years of their lives, holding themselves back because of what happened.”

This movement, it must be said, is not exclusive to women. Far from it. While most facilitators and movement leaders are women, the people seeking help are split evenly between men and women, says Sarah Hueniken, 52, an alpine guide who cofounded Mountain Muskox, which runs in-person peer-support groups, after losing a good friend to an avalanche at one of her ice-climbing camps. Several men are also on her organization’s board of directors. Jamison, too, reports that SOAR’s workshops and support groups, while fairly balanced, are mostly composed of women.

WHEN STILWELL LOGGED on to her first group session with SOAR, she was apprehensive, wary, and unsure what to expect—which Fiebig says is normal. “I didn’t know whether people would have similar experiences to me or not,” Stilwell says. “I remember asking, ‘Is there space for grief here, or is it focused on trauma?’ ”

Fiebig told her that everyone in the group had lost someone in an accident and had a paired experience of both grief and trauma. Thank God. I found the right place, Stilwell thought.

Fiebig explains that a shared lived experience allows people to talk freely about what happened without feeling the need to hold back in order to protect others in the group. But before anyone is expected to share stories, Fiebig offers some psychoeducation on trauma and grief. She talks about the nervous system, fight-or-flight, dissociation, and other physical and emotional symptoms, which Stilwell called “epiphanies that validated how I was feeling.” Eventually, Fiebig says, members begin taking the group where it needs to go, turning it into “a kind of living space” with Fiebig there to ground and guide.

Peer support has been associated with reduced isolation and improved well-being, and it has helped survivors find an enhanced capacity for meaning after traumatic events, per research. It also provides perspective in introducing people to others at different points in their journeys, offering both validation and hope. And it allows for reciprocity. “Unlike traditional models of care that position individuals primarily as recipients, peer-based approaches enable a more fluid exchange. Individuals who are further along in their process can support those who are earlier, while continuing to engage with their own experience,” write Chenoweth and her fellow authors in their paper.

SOAR is currently training a new cohort of outdoor trauma–informed mental health professionals. And every peer-support group that SOAR and Mountain Muskox run creates new ambassadors who can help the next people in the community suffering from trauma and grief. Thus the movement—like all effective groundswells—is meant to be culturally transformative, changing the way we understand the motivations for connecting to nature through risky endeavors and the way we show care and support for people in the aftermath of the unthinkable.

ALONG WITH ATTENDING the support group, Stilwell is undergoing somatic experiencing therapy to address trauma and stress held in the body and nervous system.

“A lot of my trauma is on my left side, because that’s how I was lying in the snow, and my body remembered that,” Stilwell says. “I found it really hard to lie in bed on my left side. I was immediately anxious, my heart rate went up, my breathing pattern changed.”

Stilwell’s practitioner guided her in small movements and exercises that helped to desensitize her physical responses. Some practitioners, like Brooke Edwards, a resiliency coach who works with SOAR, do visualization and meditation and occasionally even take survivors back to the environments of their trauma to help them reconnect to nature through somatic exercises.

Stilwell might join the next support group that SOAR runs, because the path to healing is not linear. “There’s no end date to this,” she says. “I think Western culture sees grief as something that needs to be healed, not something that needs to be carried. You have to carry it with you your whole life. There’s no healing from it. Somebody who had a huge influence on my life is no longer there. I’ve had to relearn who I am on my own.”

She still has nightmares and wrestles with hypervigilance. She still grapples with whether she had enough experience to be out there that day. “It’s inevitable that you ask yourself, ‘If I had been the strongest, most fit, most practiced, well-trained person, could things have been different?’ I’ll never have the answer to that question. I don’t think the answer is always yes. Ultimately, Mother Nature is more powerful than us.”

But she went back to work in April. And while she’ll never ice-climb again, she says, she’s relearning her passion for playing in the outdoors, where she discovers so much capacity to see beauty and feels connected to Wybrow. He was the one who instilled that love in her. She feels she’s out there for both of them now.

This is also the first time Stilwell has shared her story publicly. It’s daunting, to say the least. “Connecting with people who have been through something similar has been one of the most useful things to me,” she says. “I feel like I’m ready to pay it forward. And if my story could help someone else, then it’s worth sharing. If I hadn’t found some of these resources…I don’t want to say I wouldn’t be here, but it could look very different than it does.”

#4892. 5 Best Acupressure Pens for Targeted Massage, According to Experts

Here’s how to use one, and what to expert.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

There's a lot coming at you on a daily basis to stress you out. But even though you probably lean into the big de-stressors like exercising regularly, doing breathing exercises on demand, and talk therapy as needed, sometimes you just need a way to dial down the tension building up inside you without visiting a provider's office or hitting the gym. That's where acupressure pens come in.

These handheld tools, which are sometimes called acupuncture pens, are designed to target pressure points in your body to help relieve tension and pain. "Acupressure stimulates acupuncture points without using needles," says Tom Ingegno, DACM, acupuncturist and founder of Charm City Integrative Health. "It lets people take a more active role in their own health without necessarily seeing a licensed [acupuncture] practitioner."

An acupressure pen has a shape that's optimized to stimulate acupuncture points, or areas on the body that are linked to certain health benefits, explains Margie Navarro, DAOM, doctor of acupuncture at Vivacity Healthcare in New York City. "The tool has a rather small head that is smooth and rounded, so that it is a relatively comfortable way to stimulate pressure on a small area or point," she says.

People use these tools to ease anxiety, headaches, and general pain, and there is some data to suggest acupressure in general may be helpful in treating all of these. (Because each acupressure pen is slightly different, it's a little tricky to prove that they'll work for these issues.)

Still, acupuncture experts say these pens are unlikely to hurt if you want to give them a try. "It gives people a way to play an active role in their health," Navarro says. "Even just a sense of agency can improve health outcomes." Sounds like something you can get behind? These acupressure pens can get you started.

There are a ton of acupressure pens out there to choose from, and most can be used all over your body. Odacite's Mon Ami tool was specifically designed with facial acupressure in mind, with a rounded tip on one end and a spatula-scoop hybrid on the other. That allows users to apply products like moisturizers and serums to targeted areas, before massaging it in.

This metal pen feels cool to the touch, creating a soothing feel as you work out muscle tension. It also comes with a pretty pink carry bag to make it easy to tote it with you while you travel. Just be aware that you'll need to clean this regularly, especially if you use it with beauty products.

Most acupressure pens are inexpensive, but the Wellgler pen is a mere $7, making it the cheapest option on our list. The acupressure pen has two different rounded heads, allowing you to really get in there for smaller areas you want to target, like TMJ muscles. But the larger end is also a good option for massaging the rest of your face, and even your sinuses.

This pen feels a little weightier than you'd expect for $7—that can be a pro or a con, depending on your personal preference in an acupressure pen. It also has contoured grips on both ends, so you can get a comfortable, secure grasp while massaging or pressing on any given area.

The big draw of an acupressure pen is its tips—they're what you use to target pressure points, after all. But the Feelfree acupressure pen has a long, tapered tip that you can use to roll over various parts of your body, giving you even more options than "just" acupressure.

The dual rounded ends feature different sizes, so you can target your TMJ muscles with one end, before easing tension in your neck with the other, larger end. It comes with a microfiber cloth for easy cleaning, along with a travel bag, so you can easily do acupressure on the go.

Most acupressure pens you'll find are made of some kind of metal, both for a cooling feel against your skin and for ease of cleaning. The Yutiann acupressure pen is made of wood for a gentler feel. This acupressure pen is relatively large, at 6.1 centimeters, giving you more options for use.

You can use the pen and its length on your hands and face, along with your back and feet. Multiple grooves near the top of the pen create a molded feel for a comfortable grip that you may not get as easily with smaller metal pens. Just be aware that wooden tools aren't as easy to clean as their metal counterparts. This pen's larger size also means the smaller tip may not be petite enough to target teeny tense muscles.

This Rena Chris set gives you a little of everything for working out stress and pain in your face. It features a contoured acupressure pen, along with a gua sha tool, both made of a sturdy stainless steel. So, you can do targeted acupressure, followed by gua sha to ease tension and shuttle away swelling.

This set has a reflexology guide to show various pressure points on your hands, feet, and ears that you may want to touch to soothe whatever ails you. It also comes with a cleaning cloth to make clean-up a breeze. Just be aware that there's no included travel bag, making you on your own for that one.

You have a few options for use with an acupressure pen. In general, these are designed to stimulate pressure points in your body. Most people use acupressure pens for some type of pain relief, whether it's headaches or TMJ discomfort. But these pens can also be used to ease anxiety and stress.

Many acupressure pens are made of medical-grade stainless steel. However, some are made from brass or other metals. You can also find acupressure pens made of wood, although these are less common.

Every pen is slightly different, making it important to read the manufacturer's directions first. But you can typically clean an acupressure pen by wiping it with a soft cloth before you use it.

Acupressure pens shouldn't break your budget, and most cost $25 or less. "The key is the stimulation of the point, not necessarily the tool you're using," Ingegno says. "You don't need an expensive device to practice acupressure, but a pen can make it easier."

There is data to suggest that acupressure can help with easing a range of pain and discomfort. "Manual pressure can have therapeutic benefits in a variety of conditions, including muscular pain," says Navarro. But you need to know which areas to target. And, of course, not everyone will feel pain or stress relief from acupressure, regardless of whether you get it from a pen or a provider.

Ingegno suggests learning about pressure points in the body before using an acupressure pen. "I used to recommend books, but these days there's so much information online that it's pretty easy to find a starting point," he says. Once you've figured out the area you want to target, he suggests applying gentle to moderate pressure for about 30 to 60 seconds. "Some points may feel a little sore or tender when pressed, and that's not necessarily a bad thing, but you shouldn't be causing yourself pain," Ingegno says. "More pressure isn't always better."

You can apply steady pressure on a point or gently rub or massage the area with the tool, according to Ingegno. "Neither approach is wrong, and both can be useful," he says.

There are electronic acupressure pens, which deliver small electrical impulses to pressure points. "Follow the manufacturer's instructions, since there are several different types available and they don't all work the same way," Ingegno says.

Most people can safely use acupressure pens, according to Ingegno. But there are a few caveats. If you're pregnant, he recommends taking a pass. If you're using blood thinners, Ingegno also suggests being gentle, since you may bruise more easily. "Electronic acupressure pens also require a few additional precautions," Ingegno says. "People with pacemakers or other implanted electronic medical devices should avoid electrical stimulation unless their healthcare provider has specifically cleared them."

If you have broken skin or areas where the tissue is already damaged, Navarro recommends avoiding using the acupressure pen on that area.

#4891. A Former College Athlete’s Battle With Depression

He spent years trying to power through his depression, cycling through several traditional oral antidepressants, before finding a medication that worked for him.

JEREMIAH FELT GLUED to his couch, too sad and unmotivated to move. He was supposed to be getting ready for his wedding—a day when he expected to feel more confident than ever. Instead, his groomsmen had to come to his apartment and help him get there. A former college athlete, Jeremiah was still a big guy, and it took all of them to lift him from the couch and carry him out the door.

It’s not what you think. Jeremiah had absolutely no doubts about marrying the love of his life. He was in the throes of a depressive episode, one of many he had experienced dating back several years. For Jeremiah, becoming a husband meant becoming a provider and protector. But on the day he was supposed to step into that role, he was the one who needed help—and he felt ashamed.

The wedding-day episode was just one part of a much longer struggle. Jeremiah’s symptoms first appeared in college and worsened after graduation. When he entered the workforce, his symptoms worsened and he became exhausted and increasingly apathetic—to the point of neglecting his hygiene. Eventually, he became too depressed to get out of bed in the morning and lost his first job.

In 2012, Jeremiah was officially diagnosed with major depressive disorder (MDD), a mental health condition that can have a significant impact on daily life and make it difficult to find motivation or energy for self-care. Over the next nine years, persistent symptoms made it difficult for him to maintain employment, and he eventually went on disability.

DEPRESSION IN MEN often hides in plain sight. In 2021, 6.2 percent of U.S. adult men and 10.3 percent of U.S. adult women experienced a major depressive episode, according to the National Institute of Mental Health.

Those numbers tell us how common depression is, but not what it looks like. Men and women can experience many of the same symptoms, including sadness, hopelessness, fatigue, changes in sleep, and loss of interest in favorite activities. However, depression often shows up differently in men. Feeling sad or emotional isn’t always the main symptom. For many men, symptoms can show up as headaches, digestive problems, tiredness, irritability, or long-term pain. Feeling isolated or seeking distractions to avoid dealing with feelings or relationships can also be signs.

According to Craig Chepke, MD, DFAPA, a psychiatrist and medical director based in Huntersville, North Carolina, men may have a hard time talking about their feelings and asking for help, making diagnosis and treatment difficult. “Depression in men is often missed or misread, including by men and others close to them, because it doesn’t always look like what people expect depression to look like,” he explains. “Instead of sadness, it may show up as irritability, anger, withdrawal, or self-medication. Sometimes it takes an ultimatum from someone who cares about them just to get them into the office. Depression is a medical condition, not a character flaw, but I hear men with depression say variations of the same thing over and over: ‘If I was just stronger, I’d be able to handle this on my own.’”

Jeremiah agrees. “You feel like less of a man, like you should be able to just power through somehow, or snap out of it,” he says. “But you can’t. You don’t. Depression affects your confidence in every aspect of your life. It becomes a dehumanizing experience.”

BEYOND HIS OWN self-doubt, Jeremiah had a hard time finding healthcare providers who would take his symptoms seriously. He dealt with therapists who minimized his struggles. One provider even attributed his symptoms to restless legs syndrome.

At times, Jeremiah felt that some doctors viewed depression as a “woman’s disease,” subtly calling his masculinity into question. Being a Black man added another layer as he navigated a healthcare system that didn’t always understand his experience.

He experienced more difficulty when he opened up to loved ones. “Being a man is lonely in general. There are very few men you can talk to beneath the surface level about things even though you call each other friends. I shared my struggle with MDD with my two closest friends, and it kind of freaked them out,” he says. “We didn’t talk much after that for about a year.” He received a similar reaction from cousins and extended family members, who weren’t sure what to say or whether to treat him differently. Things improved once they saw that his personality hadn’t fundamentally changed.

Jeremiah’s marriage, however, became a turning point. His wife, a clinical therapist, was uniquely positioned to recognize his condition. Starting around 2016, she began noticing subtle changes, how he would pick up and lose interest in activities and hobbies, and how Jeremiah would withdraw into himself around the house. It was then that she encouraged him to seek professional help. But asking for help was only the beginning. Finding a treatment that adequately addressed his symptoms would take years.

IN 2021, JEREMIAH was diagnosed with treatment-resistant depression (TRD), which affects about 30 percent of people with MDD. TRD is generally defined as MDD that has not resolved after trying at least two traditional oral antidepressants. “By the time someone checks off medication after medication on an intake form, they’ve usually lost something more valuable than time,” Dr. Chepke says of people living with TRD. “They’ve lost hope that anything can get better.”

Jeremiah knew his feelings were real. “TRD is a bully and it will hit you in the face from the moment you wake up,” he says. “Your best days are not behind you. You’re just going through something that a lot of men go through and just aren't able to admit it. You’re working to hold onto the life you want to live, not just your health, but your lifestyle, who you want to be, and the type of man you want to become or already are.”

For a while, Jeremiah kept trying new medications and started losing hope when they didn’t work. But with help from his wife and doctor, he found a different path.

LOOKING BACK, WHAT mattered most to Jeremiah was his wife’s consistent support through the process. In the early years of treatment, she helped him remember appointments and his medication schedules that kept him moving forward when motivation was scarce. Jeremiah’s doctor recommended he try SPRAVATO® (esketamine), an FDA-approved nasal spray for adults with TRD, used alone or with an oral antidepressant.

It is not known if SPRAVATO® is safe and effective for use in preventing suicide or in reducing suicidal thoughts or actions. SPRAVATO® is not for use in place of hospitalization if your healthcare provider determines that hospitalization is needed, even if improvement is experienced after the first dose of SPRAVATO®. SPRAVATO® is not for use as a medicine to prevent or relieve pain (anesthetic). It is not known if SPRAVATO® is safe or effective as an anesthetic medicine. It is not known if SPRAVATO® is safe and effective in children. (Please see additional Important Safety Information including Boxed WARNINGS, limitations of use, and a list of side effects below. Click here to learn more.)

SPRAVATO is only available through a restricted distribution program called the SPRAVATO Risk Evaluation & Mitigation Strategy (REMS). SPRAVATO can only be administered at a certified healthcare setting, and patients self-administer the pre-filled nasal device at a REMS-certified treatment center under direct clinical supervision and are monitored for at least two hours after taking SPRAVATO. SPRAVATO may have serious side effects such as sedation, dissociation, and respiratory depression, and the risk of abuse and misuse.

SPRAVATO represents a different treatment approach for TRD. Unlike traditional antidepressants that work on serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine, SPRAVATO acts on glutamate, a chemical messenger in the brain that is thought to regulate depression. The role of glutamate in depression and the exact way SPRAVATO works are unknown.

As his depressive symptoms improved, Jeremiah began to engage more with others. He also joined a support group for Black men navigating these challenges. Hearing other people’s stories reminds him that he’s not alone. Today, he works as an IT and cybersecurity instructor in Chicago, speaks at industry conferences, and builds robots in his spare time.

Jeremiah’s experience is his own, and treatment decisions are personal. “There’s no one treatment that’s right for everybody,” Dr. Chepke says. In his practice, Dr. Chepke has witnessed reductions in certain patients’ depressive symptoms when incorporating SPRAVATO into their treatment. While not all of his patients may benefit, seeing some move from repeatedly cycling through different treatments to an option studied specifically for TRD has helped shape how he approaches care for this population.

If you haven’t found relief from your depressive symptoms, talk with your doctor about the options that may be appropriate for you—and most importantly, know that there is hope.

#4889. Your Guide to the 2026 NWSL Playoffs: Teams, Schedule, and How to Watch

After a long season, the stage is set for the National Women’s Soccer League playoffs. Eight teams will compete to see who will be crowned the 2026 champions at the end of the month. And there's been plenty of impressive soccer leading up to this point.

This year, the Washington Spirit's Ashley Sanchez tied the single-season league record with 20 goals to get the Golden Boot award. (Croix Bethune of the Kansas City Current set a league record for the most assists, too.)

Angel City FC went into the postseason with an impressive 10-match unbeaten streak, making them a big team to watch. The Seattle Reign also locked down the 8th spot in the playoffs in dramatic fashion with a 1-0 win over the Orlando Pride.

There were also big changes made to future player contracts, with the NWSL dropping the so-called "Rodman rule" that allows any player in the league to earn the NWSL's highest possible salaries. That goes into effect on January 1.

Finally, the regular season wrapped up with Decision Day on November 1, in which all of the final games kick off at once (whoa). When all was said and done, Gotham FC won the NWSL Shield—more on that in a minute—and all remaining teams locked in their seeding for playoffs.

So, which teams are in contention and how is this all going to go down? Whether you've never seen a NWSL game or need to brush up on the facts, we've got you covered.

The NWSL hosts single-elimination playoffs, which means if a team loses once, they're out. You can compare this to the NFL, whereas leagues like the WNBA, NBA, NHL, and MLB play a best-of series in each round to give teams multiple chances to advance.

This is a little confusing, so bear with us. The NWSL Shield is a regular-season honor that culminates at the end of the year.

The Shield is given to the team that has the best record over the regular season, which began back in March. Now, the playoffs begin, and the winner of the playoff tournament wins the NWSL Championship. It's possible to win both the Shield and the Championship, btw. It's just that the Shield is a distinction for regular season play. (Gotham FC won the NWSL Championship in 2023 and 2025, but only won the club’s first-ever Shield this season.)

The team that wins the Shield (in this case, Gotham) is also granted the No. 1 seed in the playoffs, which means they get home-field advantage during the postseason.

If there's a tie in the NWSL playoffs, the game will go on to extra time. This is two 15-minute periods that are played in their entirety. Whoever has the highest score at the end wins.

If things are still tied at that point, this goes to a penalty shootout. This is a best of five round of kicks, followed by sudden-death rounds if they're needed.

The first round of the playoffs will be broadcast on ESPN platforms, along with Prime Video, CBS, and Paramount+. The semifinals, which take place November 14-15, will be broadcast on ESPN networks, CBS, and Paramount+. The championship game will air on CBS and Paramount+.

You might even consider visiting a dedicated women’s sports bar in your area to watch with other like-minded fans—here’s an exhaustive list.

Eight teams are in contention this year. Here they are, as well as their seeds going into the first round:

The championship game is on Saturday, Nov. 21 at 8 pm ET. Last year’s championship game saw Gotham FC beat the Washington Spirt 1-0 with a goal at the 80th minute. The stage is set for an equally exciting finale to the NWSL season.

#4888. What Rest-Pause Training Can Do for Your Workout

A simple practice lets you push past failure—without lowering the weight.

TRY AS YOU might, you can’t pump out reps forever when you’re working toward building bigger muscles. Eventually, you‘ll be too fatigued to complete another rep with good form, a point referred to as “technical failure.” Pushing beyond your last good rep can lead to sloppy lifting mechanics, which can compromise your results or, worse increase your risk of injury. If you find yourself stuck lifting the same weight for the same reps, it may be time to get creative with how you push past that iron hurdle.

One way to head off the siren song of ego lifting is by implementing a planned rest-pause set. It’s an intense lifting technique that requires focus and intention, and as effective as it can be, it shouldn’t be done for every set or even every exercise.

By briefly resting after reaching failure, you can squeeze out a few more quality reps using the same weight. A few extra reps might not seem like a big deal, but they can add up over time, giving your muscles an extra dose of the tension that drives growth.

To do a rest-pause set, you’ll take an exercise to the point where you can’t complete another rep with good form. You’ll then rest for five to 15 seconds—in one MH workout plan, fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. recommends taking “three deep breaths” for a pause—then squeeze out a few more reps (expect to be able to do two to four) using the same weight. You can repeat this process, though one additional round of reps is a good starting point.

If you rest longer than 20 seconds, Alexander Rothstein, an exercise physiologist and program coordinator of exercise science at the New York Institute of Technology, says you’re starting to approach a standard rest interval. "If you give yourself that brief moment to… recover, and then you continue the set, you haven't flushed away all of the waste products, and you haven't fully recovered your energy stores, but you are still capable of doing a few more high-quality reps,” he explains.

The purpose of a rest-pause set is to push your muscle to complete a few more hard (but high-quality) reps. If you’re aiming to build muscle, it’s those hard reps near the end of a set that are key; a rest-pause set allows you to sneak in a few more of those reps. While lifters of any experience level can perform rest-pause sets, they’re especially useful for advanced lifters who’ve already cashed in their newbie gains and find it increasingly difficult to progress their lifts and add muscle.

Say you’re doing the dumbbell bench press, an exercise on which you’ve been stuck using the same 50-pound dumbbells for sets of 8 to 10 reps for over a month. You get to that 10th rep and, once again, can’t muster another. Instead of calling it this time, you’ll sit up, rest the dumbbells on your thighs for 15 seconds, and then bust out another two reps. Congrats. You just eked out more worthwhile reps, which, over time, should help you progress.

“But isn’t that cheating?” you ask. No—and even if it were, there are times when cheating pays off for muscle gains. And research suggests that traditional sets and rest-pause sets can produce similar gains in strength and muscle. One small study had 18 experienced lifters perform six weeks of traditional sets or rest-pause training with the same relative load. One group completed three sets of six reps; the other did one set to failure and then as many rest-pause sets as necessary to hit 18 reps. Both groups achieved similar strength gains, but the rest-pause group experienced greater increases in thigh muscle thickness and leg-press muscular endurance.

As for how to start using them, pick one exercise per workout—ideally, a move you’re struggling to progress—and do the final set of that exercise as a rest-pause set. This often works best with the final exercise in your workout. The rest-pause protocol can be downright exhausting, and using them too early may compromise your ability to hit your typical reps and weights during subsequent sets.

One note: You can perform rest-pause sets with just about any exercise, but there are two places where they’re especially beneficial. Weight machines are the safest, letting you easily push to fatigue, then take your brief “rest”. Exercises that offer support for stabilizing muscles (think: chest-supported rows) also work well. And many single-joint free-weight exercises, like dumbbell curls are good options. If you’re going to attempt a rest-pause set with the bench press or back squat, have a good spotter on hand.

There’s more than one way to increase the volume of a single set, and these methods are often referred to as intensity techniques. Below, we’ll briefly compare the three most popular ones to rest-pause sets.

A drop set is when you reach failure on a lift, then immediately reduce the load (often by 10 to 20 percent) and try to squeeze out a few more reps. In many ways, it’s similar to a rest-pause set, but because you’re lightening the weight, you’ll find it easier to maintain good form.

“Personally, I just like the volume approach of drop sets,” Rothstein says. "When you do drop sets, obviously the load is being reduced, so it's not as potentially strength beneficial as it might be to just do rest-pauses and still lift heavy loads."

A cluster set is when you break up a traditional straight set into a series of mini sets, or clusters, with short rest periods between each. They're a popular training method among strength athletes, such as powerlifters and weightlifters, who want to accumulate more total tonnage.

Say, for example, you can typically deadlift 250 pounds for eight reps. You could load 285 to 300 pounds on the bar and perform four two-rep clusters, resting 15 to 30 seconds between, to complete the same eight reps with roughly 15 to 20 percent more weight.

The main difference between rest-pause and cluster sets is that cluster sets strategically use rest to achieve a preplanned number of reps, often at a higher weight. Rest-pause sets have you take a few breaths after reaching failure to push past what you can normally do rep-wise. Cluster sets are likely superior to rest-pause sets for building strength.

Instead of resting and then doing more reps once you reach failure, you can perform forced reps, where your spotter provides just enough assistance to help you complete a few more reps with good form. Forced reps are usually done on exercises where a spotter can easily help; think the bench press or certain machine exercises, not deadlifts or heavy back squats.

While you’re technically pushing past failure, you don’t have control over how much assistance your spotter provides; this can vary from workout to workout or even rep to rep. You can, however, control the eccentric portion of the contraction after the spotter has helped you, so if you’re doing forced reps, it’s a must to lower the weight slowly to get the most from these. Forced reps can be a useful occasional technique if you have an experienced spotter who knows how much assistance to provide; because they’re forcing you to acclimate to increased time-under-tension with a weight that you know is challenging.

#4887. Wellness Apps, Medically Tailored Meals Help Slow Weight Gain After GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Weight regain is common after stopping GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide (Wegovy, Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound).

In fact, previous research has shown that most people regain at least half of their lost weight within 1 year of stopping treatment, with weight regain often accelerating during the first 3–4 months.

However, a new study suggests that structured support, including a weight management app or medically tailored meals, may help slow weight regain after discontinuing GLP-1 medications.

The small study, published October 7 in Obesity Science & Practice, found that participants who received either intervention regained significantly less weight over four months than those receiving usual care.

The study included 39 adults with an average age of 50, an average weight of 189 pounds, and an average body mass index (BMI) of 31.4.

All participants had lost more than 10% of their body weight while taking GLP-1 medications and had stopped treatment within the previous 30 days.

All participants also completed questionnaires at the beginning and end of the study and used Bluetooth scales to track their weight at home throughout the four-month period.

Researchers randomly assigned participants to one of the following three groups:

Participants continued to receive care from their healthcare providers, which may include nutrition, exercise, and lifestyle counseling from a clinician or registered dietitian. The type and amount of support varied depending on the provider’s recommendations and available resources. The researchers did not provide any additional intervention.

Participants received a subscription to Noom, an app that uses behavioral strategies to support weight loss and maintenance. These include tracking food intake, exercise, and weight, as well as educational lessons on the psychological, physiological, social, and environmental factors that influence eating behaviors.

The app also provides tools to help users recognize and manage triggers that may lead to overeating. Participants were encouraged to use the app for at least 15 minutes daily, including completing lessons, logging food, and tracking their weight.

These are typically nutrient-dense meals developed by registered dietitians to meet the nutritional needs of people with specific health conditions, such as chronic kidney disease or uncontrolled type 2 diabetes.

For this study, participants in this group selected 10 portion-controlled, “weight wellness” meals each week from more than 70 options, which were delivered to their homes.

After four months, participants who received either medically tailored meals or access to the digital weight management app experienced significantly less weight regain than those receiving usual care.

The estimated weight regain was 10.75% of body weight in the usual-care group, compared with 3.6% in the Noom group and 3.58% in the medically tailored meals group.

Although participants in all three groups regained weight, the findings suggest that structured nutritional or behavioral support may help limit weight regain after stopping GLP-1 medications.

“These findings highlight the benefits of ongoing support for patients on a weight loss journey,” said Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA. Ali wasn’t involved in the study.

Denise Pate, MD, a board certified internist with Medical Offices of Manhattan who was also not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are significant “because they show that obesity management is multifactorial, not only medication, but the combination of types of meals and behavioral change all play a role.”

However, because this was a small, four-month study, larger, longer-term trials are needed to determine whether these approaches can help people maintain weight loss over time after stopping GLP-1 medications.

Ali noted that research suggests GLP-1 medications are most effective for weight management when taken long-term.

“Obesity needs to be recognized and treated as a chronic condition, similar to diabetes or hypertension,” he said.

Pate agreed, emphasizing that obesity is not always recognized as a chronic condition that may require ongoing treatment.

“I feel that the medical community, insurance, and the population as a whole have yet to fully accept obesity as a chronic medical condition, which it most definitely is for a large part of patients. For this reason, I think patients should stay on these medications long term if needed,” she said.

“GLP-1 medications are highly effective tools for transitioning to a healthier diet and lifestyle, which for most people may require long-term use,” Ali added.

Pate explained that one of the goals of GLP-1 medications is to help people eat smaller portions by recognizing when they feel full and stopping when they do.

“I tell my patients from the start, this is the goal,” she said, adding that she hopes patients will retain those habits after stopping treatment.

Ali recommended maintaining a balanced diet rich in protein and vegetables while limiting added sugars and refined carbohydrates.

He added that tracking apps and regular follow-up appointments with a healthcare professional or registered dietitian may also help people maintain their progress.

“Patients need to understand that the GLP medication is not a miracle drug, although with the dramatic weight loss, it can be perceived as such. It is only a tool to be used in conjunction with an exercise routine as well as a healthy diet,” Pate said.

Chapped lips are a real bummer this time of year. They’re uncomfy and unsightly—and often feel inevitable thanks to cold weather and dry indoor air. #4884. Scientists Were Shocked to Discover Yet Another Surprising Benefit of Cranberry Juice

Cranberry juice is known in certain circles as a helpful way to prevent the risk of future UTIs, but there's more to this beverage than that. Now, new research suggests the drink could also help your teeth...or at least help reduce plaque associated with tooth decay.

The study, which was published in the journal Scientific Reports, found that 100 percent cranberry juice could slow the growth of dental plaque and reduce the production of certain acids that could lead to cavities.

It's important to stress that the findings are preliminary at this point. But dentists say the idea of using cranberry juice to lower the odds of tooth decay isn't as out there as it seems. Here's the deal.

Meet the experts: Mark S. Wolff, DDS, PhD, dean at the University of Pennsylvania School of Dental Medicine; Christine D. Wu, PhD, lead study author and professor in the Department of Pediatric Dentistry at the University of Illinois Chicago; Julie Meyerson, DMD, a dentist in New York City; and Matthew J. Messina, DDS, clinical associate professor at The Ohio State University College of Dentistry

For the study, researchers recruited 22 people (eight adults and 14 kids) and randomly assigned them one of three drinks: unsweetened 100 percent cranberry juice, cranberry juice cocktail (made up of 27 percent juice and added sugar), or water.

The participants didn't brush their teeth the morning of the experiment. To start, researchers collected dental plaque samples that had accumulated overnight with cotton swabs. The participants then rinsed their mouths with water, before having three small amounts of their assigned drink, swishing each around their mouths several times before swallowing.

After 30 minutes, the researchers took plaque samples again. (This time, they took samples from teeth that hadn't been swabbed earlier.) The researchers discovered that people who swished with and drank pure cranberry juice had slower plaque regrowth than those who didn't use the drink.

The pure cranberry juice was also linked with less acid production in dental plaque. (The acids made by oral bacteria can break down tooth enamel and increase the risk of cavities.)

Again, the study was small, so much more research is needed. And though the decision to study cranberry juice for oral health seems random, there's some precedent, according to Christine D. Wu, PhD, lead study author and professor in the Department of Pediatric Dentistry at the University of Illinois Chicago. "[Cranberry juice] has a polyphenol chemical compound called proanthocyanidin," she says. During research on the compound, Wu says her team discovered that proanthocyanidin can impact dental plaque.

"These compounds may interfere with processes involved in plaque formation," says Julie Meyerson, DMD, a dentist in New York City. For example, bacteria like Streptococcus mutans produce enzymes that convert dietary sugars into sticky substances called glucans, which help bacteria attach to teeth and form plaque biofilms, she says. "Cranberry polyphenols may interfere with these processes, making it more difficult for bacteria to adhere and form mature biofilms on teeth," Meyerson says. (That biofilm is also known as plaque.)

Cranberry compounds may also influence the metabolism of bacteria and reduce acid production as a result, she says. "This is important because acids produced by plaque bacteria lower the oral pH, contributing to enamel demineralization and tooth decay," Meyerson says.

Matthew J. Messina, DDS, clinical associate professor at The Ohio State University College of Dentistry, agrees that the proanthocyanidins are likely fueling this link. "These are the same compounds associated with cranberry’s reputation for urinary tract health," he says. "Proanthocyanidins don’t so much kill bacteria as interfere with them."

What we don't know right now is how this will actually impact dental health. "It could very well suppress plaque, but will it affect disease?" says Mark S. Wolff, DDS, PhD, dean at the University of Pennsylvania School of Dental Medicine. "The findings are very preliminary."

Wu says that cranberry juice "may be a functional food" for dental health, but more research is needed.

Messina agrees. If you like cranberry juice, he recommends having unsweetened 100 percent juice over a cranberry juice cocktail. But at the same time, "don’t trade your toothbrush for a juice glass," he says. " Brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, cleaning between teeth, limiting sugar, and seeing your dentist regularly are still what prevent cavities."

#4883. Volkswagen gets L3 autonomous driving test permit in China, eyes 2027

Volkswagen Group China now has a permit to test Level 3 autonomous driving on public roads in Hefei, and it says testing is already underway. The permit also covers large-scale driving data collection in the city.

It’s the latest step toward VW’s goal of L3 technology readiness in China by 2027. And the timing is good as the group holds its first China Technology Day in Hefei on Wednesday.

VW says the permit was issued under China’s strictest L3 framework and that its setup meets the country’s latest mandatory safety design standards. It didn’t say which authority issued it, how many vehicles are in the fleet, or which roads they can use.

Hefei makes sense as a base. It’s home to the Volkswagen China Technology Company (VCTC), the group’s largest R&D center outside Germany, and to its Volkswagen Anhui production site.

The software comes from CARIZON, VW’s intelligent driving unit in China, which started as a joint venture between CARIAD and Horizon Robotics. Its driver assistance system is called Hyper Sense 8 (HS8), which VW describes as its first “full-scenario” ADAS.

Behind it is GAIA 2.0, a world model VW built itself. VW says it runs simulation equal to 5 million km of safety testing per day, using about 30 million real-road scenario clips, and it wants to get that to 10 million km per day. VW is also developing its own system-on-chip, the C7H, which it says can support up to Level 4.

Ralf Brandstätter, chairman and CEO of Volkswagen Group China, kept the message on safety. He said the group “will never advance technology at the cost of safety” and called the permit an important step on the road to L3 readiness (our translation from Chinese).

This is a road test permit. VW can’t sell L3 cars to customers with it.

China’s MIIT granted the country’s first L3 product approvals in December 2025 to two sedans: a Changan model capped at 50 km/h on designated Chongqing expressways, and a BAIC Arcfox model capped at 80 km/h on three Beijing routes. GAC’s Hyptec and XPeng already hold L3 road test permits too. So VW isn’t leading here. It’s catching up to Chinese brands on their home turf.

In July, VW, CARIZON, and Horizon Robotics said they would deepen their partnership, giving CARIZON “white-box” access to Horizon’s AI foundation model, and targeted the start of L3 deliveries in the second half of 2027. VW’s L2++ system is rolling out on seven new NEV models from its Chinese joint ventures this year.

VW also leans on XPeng in China. It bought a roughly 5% stake in XPeng in 2023 and co-developed its China zonal electrical architecture, CEA, with the startup.

Outside China, the only Western automaker with a certified L3 system on sale is Mercedes-Benz, whose Drive Pilot works on approved highways in Germany and in California and Nevada. Mercedes also got approval to test Level 4 driving in Beijing back in 2024. Tesla’s FSD remains a Level 2 system everywhere it’s sold, China included.

L3 is where liability moves. When the system is engaged, the automaker is responsible for the driving, not the person in the seat. That’s why so few companies have shipped it, and why the ones that have keep it on a short leash: specific roads, low speeds, mostly traffic jams.

China has been serious about building a framework for automakers to bring this techonology to market, and through it, we are seeing who is interested in this version of autonomy.

Not everyone is. Many automakers, including Tesla, have been talking about “skipping” level 3 and going straight to level 4.

#4882. Matt Damon and David Letterman Pop into The Gilded Age Just for Funzies

HBO’s period drama got a very modern surprise from two very recognizable faces.

IF YOU’RE NOT familiar with HBO’s The Gilded Age, it’s a pretty easy show to explain. Set in New York City during the titular era—the rapidly changing 1880s—the show is an exploration of the rich-people trials and tribulations of a new money family (led by Carrie Coon and Morgan “Train Daddy” Spector) and their neighbors, an old money family (led by Christine Baranski).

One of the show’s most important aspects is its production design, with intricately built sets and elaborately planned costumes helping to transport its viewers back nearly 150 years. Immersion is the name of the game.

With a setup like that, The Gilded Age is just about the last show where you’d expect to see a couple of our most recognizable modern stars walk directly across the screen—but that’s just what Matt Damon and David Letterman did, less than 10 minutes into the show’s season 4 premiere.

Damon, the Oscar-winning movie star who earlier this year led Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey and Netflix’s The Rip, and Letterman, the legendary talk show host, walked across the screen in full costume, saying nothing, in a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it moment.

As it turns out, according to a story published by Vulture, the whole thing was born from Letterman’s lifelong desire to make a surprise appearance in something as a background actor, something that began way back in 1977 when he saw a fellow comedian friend slyly appear in the background of a scene in Annie Hall.

In recent years, Letterman has apparently come close to shooting background scenes in Wes Anderson’s The Phoenician Scheme, the upcoming Michael B. Jordan-directed version of The Thomas Crown Affair, and Black Rabbit alongside Jason Bateman—but for one reason or another, none of them came to be.

Letterman filmed an upcoming episode of his current show, the Netflix interview series My Next Guest Needs No Introduction with David Letterman, with Damon, and discovered that Damon and Ben Affleck began their careers as background actors, and, for the sake of the bit, figured this would be the perfect opportunity to see his dream come to fruition. “We thought, Okay, this could be the perfect opportunity,” Next Guest showrunner Isabel Richardson explained to Vulture. “It’d be really fun for Dave to do this with Academy Award–winner Matt Damon, and it tied into his origin story really well.”

Damon, luckily, was into the idea too—and they made it happen. “It was a kind of hysterical moment when our production supervisor Leah Baker came up to me on set and was like, ‘Well, I have a kind of funny, interesting question: Would you like Dave Letterman and Matt Damon to be background on our set one day?’” Gilded Age showrunner Churchill said in the same Vulture story. “I just started laughing.”

Surprise appearances and cameos have long been a part of Damon’s playbook. Marvel fans certainly remember his brief appearances in movies like Deadpool 2 and Thor: Ragnarok, while fans of Damon’s frequent collaborator Steven Soderbergh’s movies won’t forget his surprise turns in movies like No Sudden Move and Che: Part Two. He even appeared in a very brief role in Ethan Coen’s Drive Away Dolls after working with Ethan and his brother Joel on the 2010 hit True Grit.

Perhaps Damon’s most memorable (and truly most random) cameo comes in the 2004 comedy Eurotrip, though. He appears early in the film as Donnie, the lead singer of an alt-rock band who sings a song about the affair he was apparently having with the main character’s girlfriend. “Scotty Doesn’t Know” is a pillar of both 2000s pop-punk and that era’s teen sex comedy movement, and Damon’s completely out-of-nowhere cameo is a huge reason why.

And, look, HBO seems to enjoy this kind of thing anyway. Just last month, we spotted the University of Nebraska’s head football coach Matt Rhule in the final episode of Lanterns. Does his appearance make sense in a show set in Nebraska? Sure. Did we ever expect to see Matt Rhule in an acclaimed, highly watched HBO drama set in a superhero world? No, we certainly did not.

It’s fun (and probably a bit trippy at first) to come to grips with seeing who you think you’re seeing. And if, somehow, you don’t know who either of those two are, you probably won’t notice at all and won’t think a thing. And isn’t that how all great cameos should go, really?

#4881. BYD opens pre-orders for its first luxury electric SUV with over 1,000 km CLTC range

BYD opened pre-orders for the new Denza N8, a luxury five-seat electric SUV with a CLTC range of over 1,000 km (621 miles).

“The king of large 5-seater pure electric vehicles,” as BYD’s luxury sub-brand Denza calls it, is now available to pre-order in China.

BYD opened pre-orders for the new Denza N8 on Monday, and the results so far “have been excellent,” according to Li Hui, Denza’s general manager.

The new Denza N8 is “definitely the most anticipated luxury SUV of the year,” Li said. Denza confirmed in August that the new version will use its Blade Battery 2.0 and Flash Charging Technology to deliver “a world-leading 1,003 km pure electric range.”

Although BYD has released several luxury EVs that offer more than 1,000 km of CLTC range, such as the Denza Z9 GT, this is its first electric SUV to break the 1,000 km mark under CLTC conditions.

For context, the plug-in hybrid version the new Denza N8 is replacing offered a combined CLTC range of 1,003 km (623 miles) on a full tank of gas and a full charge.

BYD didn’t reveal pre-order prices, but Li confirmed last week that the Denza N8’s official launch is scheduled for November.

It will go on sale after the new Denza N8L, a slightly longer six-seat version. The N8L is available in two versions: Premium and Flagship. The N8L EV Premium starts at 299,800 RMB, or about $45,000, while the Flagship model is priced from 329,800 RMB ($49,000).

Those who place a reservation with a 2,000 RMB ($200) deposit will receive a 5,000 RMB credit as a limited-time special offer.

Measuring 5,150 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,820 mm high, with a 3,075 mm wheelbase, the Denza N8 EV is slightly longer than the Kia EV9 and Hyundai IONIQ 9.

Inside, the five-seat electric SUV features a massive 30″ infotainment screen that spans nearly the entire passenger-side dashboard, plus a new 43″ (1.1 meter) panoramic head-up display (PHUD) at the bottom of the windshield.

Other premium features include zero gravity seating in all rows, a three-spoke steering wheel, wireless phone chargers, and ambient lighting.

The luxury SUV is equipped with a roof-mounted LiDAR to support BYD’s God’s Eye 5.0 smart driving assistance system. It also features DiSus-A, BYD’s intelligent air suspension system, and rear-wheel drive.

The new Denza N8 EV will be available with a single rear-wheel-drive (RWD) or a tri-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain. The RWD version uses a single motor producing either 320 kW (429 hp) or 370 kW (496 hp).

The tri-motor Denza N8 uses BYD’s e3 platform. The setup includes a 270 kW (362 hp) front motor and two 310 kW (416 hp) rear motors, delivering a combined output of 890 kW (1,193 hp).

Regulatory filings earlier this year revealed it will be available with a 130.15 kWh or 105.79 kWh BYD Blade 2.0 battery, offering CLTC ranges of up to 1,003 km and 800 km, respectively.

BYD will announce prices next month, but given that the Denza N8L starts at 299,800 RMB ($45,000), the standard version will likely be priced below it.

#4880. The Fan Traditions You Need to Know This NWSL Postseason

The 2026 NWSL playoffs kick off on Friday, with single-elimination play that's guaranteed to be a nail-biter. Eight teams made the playoffs, but only one will hoist the championship trophy on November 21.

Of course, part of the fun of watching any playoff game is knowing insider-y details about each team. That includes fan traditions that make a team unique—and that you can join in on, too.

Every team has its own special chants and traditions that are uniquely theirs, and knowing what they are before kickoff immediately creates a level of familiarity you wouldn't have otherwise. You may already have "your" NWSL team that you root for, and you're probably familiar with their special traditions. But there are also likely teams you'll be watching during playoffs that you don't know the ins and outs of.

Whether you're looking for another club to root for when yours isn't playing or you just want to brush up on the details, these are the unique and sometimes hilarious fan traditions to know this NWSL postseason.

The San Diego Wave fans aren't messing around. They've formed their own supporters' group called the San Diego Sirens, and they're happy to include everyone in the club.

The Sirens have an online breakdown of songs and chants to know ahead of games. They even included helpful clips, so you can learn the melodies ahead of games. (There's a lot of water-themed content in there, making these very on-brand.)

The Utah Royals' fandom is called the Throne, and they march into the stadium as a united front before kickoff. (The Throne also says that everyone is welcome to join in.) The Royals also list their go-to chants online, allowing fans new and old to brush up before games.

Cloud 9 is Gotham's supporters club, and they've borrowed a few traditions from the UK's Manchester United. That includes incorporating John Denver’s “Take Me Home, Country Roads,” and making it “Gotham Roads,” as a tribute to the team.

You can download the club's songs on your phone and take them to the game or to your watch party to follow along.

The Royal Guard is Seattle Reign's fan club, and they've got plenty of traditions to share. The group does a walk toward Lumen Field before kickoff and incorporates a match-day band that might be the largest in NWSL. Check out their chants—with emojis to show when to clap—to get in the spirit.

The Kansas City Current has three different groups of supporters to make game day a high-energy event. That includes the KC Blue Crew, Surface Tension Drumming Club, and Undertow KC.

The organizations work together and have an online list of chants, the music they're set to, sheet music for drummers, and even videos to help fans get up to speed.

Not to be outdone, Angel City has six recognized supporter groups to cheer on its team—the most in the NWSL. Those groups regularly pack “La Fortaleza,” the supporters section. The groups share chants, and you can brush up on them online.

Rebellion 99 is Angel City's largest supporter group. Along with the other groups, they do chants and set off flares to keep the energy going. Rebellion 99 even has a scholarship program for local youth, stressing the importance of community-buildin

Washington Spirit offers four different fan clubs to choose from. One of the team's major groups, called the Spirit Squadron, marches to the stadium together before games. They also hilariously have a chant that they stole from the English Premier League called "Let’s pretend we scored a goal" when things aren't going so well.

There's also a stadium tradition: At the 51st minute, a "Free D.C." chant starts as a nod to the push for Washington, D.C., to become the 51st state.

The Portland Thorns' support groups are the Rose City Riveters and Timbers Army. They have a slew of chants you can download to follow along. In the mix: A chant called "Rose City 'Til I Die," which they do when the other team scores.
