#4819. Alan Cumming Can’t Be Tamed

At 61, the Traitors host has made a career of playing by his own rules. From leading his dark new series Tip Toe to reprising his X-Men role as Nightcrawler in Avengers: Doomsday, he's always eager to take on a different form.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

“I’M GEARING UP towards hacking it all off,” Alan Cumming says as he twists a finger around an errant silver tendril of hair dangling across his forehead. “I usually like to end a job and do something—get it cut off or get it colored. Something.”

The 61-year-old Tony-winning-Broadway-star-turned-Emmy-winning-reality-TV-host is the consummate chameleon. In just the past year, he’s played the “dandy Scottish laird” host of The Traitors: New Blood, reprised his role as the X-Men’s resident lizard-like teleporting mutant Nightcrawler in Avengers: Doomsday, and took on one of his most emotionally and physically challenging roles as gay bar owner Leo in Tip Toe.

The impulse to change—both on screen and off—is therapeutic. “Over the years, I've had so many different hairstyles, I think, as a reaction to my childhood trauma about my father's obsession with my hair,” he says. Cumming’s memoir, Not My Father’s Son, opens with a scene of his father taking a rusty pair of sheep shears to his temple in a fit of rage. “They were blunt and dirty and they cut my skin, but my father shaved my head with them, holding me down like an animal,” Cumming writes in the first chapter.

The trauma followed him into early adulthood, and he experienced visceral anxiety whenever he got his hair cut. Eventually, however, the act of transformation transformed Cumming. “Hair was always something I felt I had no control over as a child,” he says. “So I wanted to have as much control over it and change it as much as possible, almost in a slightly perverse way.”

Of course, the choice to change isn’t always his, and sometimes the choice is taken away from him. It was “painful,” he says, to be unable to change his hair when he was working on certain projects, like his seven seasons on The Good Wife. “Over the years, I've had so many different hairstyles, but I don't often have my own hair,” Cumming adds. “It's usually for some job.”

Today, however, his natural silver hair seems purposefully unstyled as his fingers coax through it. That is, when he isn’t using his hands to assume the statuesque pose of his Traitors persona or demonstrate the boxing stance from his Marvel superhero training. Simply talking about a performance becomes a performance, his eyes bulging behind a pair of thick-rimmed black glasses and his arms gesturing widely underneath his faded red T-shirt as he describes the immense physicality required of these recent roles.

The walls of his Scottish home are white and surprisingly sparse. You’d have no idea that the person living there is now, by his own admission, best known for “swanning around” a Scottish castle “like an insane little prince” in increasingly outrageous outfits (so outrageous, in fact, that Traitors contestants often applaud when he enters the room after a wardrobe change). Or perhaps the walls are white so he stands out all the more. Either way, the Scottish charm is working overtime on a Sunday evening.

“I think both with my hair and, more lately with what I wear, I do sort of feel like a little dolly that people dress up,” he says before adding, with a good-natured laugh, “I don't mind it.”

In a brief moment between transformations, Cumming sat down with Men’s Health to discuss his ever-changing style on Traitors, how he trained for Avengers: Doomsday, and what he considers to be the ultimate fountain of youth.

MEN’S HEALTH: You often talk about your fashion choices with each Traitors season, but what goes into choosing your hairstyle?

ALAN CUMMING: There was a feeling that because we were doing the civilian version, we could reboot and bring things down a little. So, we decided just to go a little more simple and classic with the hair. But it was hilarious, because every morning I would walk downstairs and say, ‘This is toning it down. What the fuck?’ I guess I wasn't dressed as a coffin or a bride. The plan was to go back to the dandy Scottish laird a little, but it still was pretty mental. But that's why I didn't have lots of color and things in my hair. But we're about to start another Traitors season in a couple of weeks, so all bets are off again.

MH: You're in your 60s now, and you still have wonderful hair. Did you ever have a fear of going bald when you were younger, or would that have maybe been freeing in a way?

AC: I've never feared going bald. I don't think I would care. It's easy when you’re not the bald person saying this, but I don't quite think going bald has the same power it used to. I feel like so many people shave their heads nowadays anyway. And there are loads of actors I know who are bald and wear wigs all the time. When you're an actor, it's obviously easier—and actually probably better—to be bald, because you get more hairdo options.

MH: Outside of Traitors, you're also reprising your role as Nightcrawler in Avengers: Doomsday. How was doing your own stunts in your 60s?

AC: I did some stunt work, but I didn't do all my own stunts. Please don't think that. There are lots of things I'm not allowed to tell you about. I got into trouble for giving the game away earlier on. But I mean, I fight some people. There's loads of fighting in it. If you enjoy fighting and you enjoy superheroes, this movie's for you.

I loved the training. They always train you for much more than you actually need, but I did it. I was boxing with these French boys. And I’d just made a film in France, so they were very impressed with my French and the fact that I could box a little and not have a heart attack.

It’s really funny when people, especially younger people, are so impressed by your fitness. I'm quite bendy as well, so people are always impressed by my flexibility. And I guess I am 61, but, I mean, I'm not dead. I'm not a thousand years old. I've luckily not had any sort of physical things going wrong. I don't really feel any different, to be honest, but it’s also hilarious when young people are just amazed that you've been able to stand up and not die.

MH: How long were you doing this boxing training for?

AC: I only did a week or so with those boys. But I used to take boxing lessons in New York, and I really want to get back into it again. It's such good exercise, especially before you actually get up and spar—all the core stuff and strength stuff—and it's such fun as well.

My boxing teacher was called Mo, and he'd been a big sort of world champion. But one day I went to the gym, and he was really pissed off because he’d seen a music video with some rappers and singers, and they were all playing boxers. He said, "They were just terrible."

And he went, "Drake. Drake was the worst."

And he said to me, "You could take Drake." So now, every time I see Drake, I just think, “I could take you.” Drake better watch out.

MH: Let him know it's on sight. How else did you prepare your body for Avengers?

AC: I actually stay pretty fit all the time. When I'm doing The Traitors, I go to the gym every day, or I do three days gym, two days swim or yoga. There have been times in my life when I've had to get really, really super fit or super skinny or something, so you go nuts. But I like being fit, and I like stretching. I like doing things like that, so I’m pretty constant.

Filming Tip Toe was much more physically demanding, because I knew I was going to have a lot of emotional weight to carry. It was a really disturbing show. So, I would exercise a lot, but I would also get two Thai massages on the weekend because my body was so tense.

If you do a film like X-Men and you're jumping around, yes, sometimes your body can get hurt in that way, but emotionally it wasn't really very demanding, whereas Tip Toe was so intense. Physically, I'm so stressed a lot of the time, and David Morrissey, the other actor, is shoving me around. So, my body was all screwed up. What's really important in those situations is to plan ahead and to make space for you to give your body some chance to recover.

MH: How do you think about your body differently as you take on each new role?

AC: I'm a very physical actor. I think about how the person physically behaves and how they move and stand and… [laughs]. I'm laughing because my husband is just over there, and he always watches me in things and says, "Oh, you look so different. You just disappeared into this character." And then there'll be a scene when I'm running, and he can tell it's me because I run in a weird way. My running always gives me away. But you know who's got the weirdest run ever? Woody Allen. I was once in a film with him and he had to run, and I've never seen anything like it. It just was like, "How is this all happening? How are all these limbs managing to propel someone forward?" It was the craziest thing.

But I'm always very conscious of the physicality of a character. The Traitors is a big example. He's very erect, very sort of grand, quite dancy. He moves like a dancer. And then in Tip Toe, it was really fascinating becoming more cowed as the show went on. He got less confident, so I got more crushed.

With Nightcrawler, he's really fascinating because he's like a little weird lizard or something. So it's a lot of neck stuff. In the first film, I did a lot of work with a movement person to develop the language of that. So, I just remembered all that stuff for Avengers. I suppose it’s muscle memory. After 22 years, I really did remember all that stuff. Also, they gave me a gray wig, which I thought was hilarious. That was a concession to my elder statesman-like thing. I've got gray hair as Nightcrawler now, which is just hilarious. Nothing else has changed, just his hair has grown gray.

MH: You mentioned your longtime husband, Grant. What do you think makes a relationship last?

AC: Having a laugh, being open and kind. Being kind is the biggest thing, but being honest and always trying to talk things through and having a laugh. Also, having time apart.

When I go away to make a film or whatever, we don't see each other for a few weeks. It's actually really great because you miss that person, and you look forward to seeing them and you value the time you do have. It's not just about missing them, but you remember the things that you've always liked, and you're constantly reassessing your relationship because you're looking forward to seeing that person again. Also, it means you maintain your own identity. Obviously, we're a very strong couple, but we have our own lives as well.

So it's a combination of those things, but I really do think you can't underestimate how much being able to laugh is. Also, I think it's good to still have sex. Sex and laughter. I think if either of those go or both of those go, get out, taxi for one. Because they're both the same thing, I suppose—they're sensual pleasures. Those are very important for me, anyway.

MH: Agreed. And so, you mentioned that you're 61 now—

MH: As we all should. But tell me, what's the best part about being 61?

AC: There are lots of nice things. I mean, partly that I forget I'm 61. On the show I'm doing right now, I feel like I can just chat with the kids on the crew who are in their 20s. For me, what's great is being in a position where I'm able to have such strong, long relationships, friendships. With Tip Toe, David Morrissey and I have known each other since the late '80s. Acting against each other in such a horrible way was so great because we were so close and trusted each other. And that was a really good thing about being older—you're so sure of someone and so trust someone. Also, I just love having a life where I do have friends in their 20s and 30s and 40s.

I equate oldness with lack of curiosity. You can be very old and still be very curious, but whenever anyone says, “Oh, I'm too old for this,” I think it's like a death knell somewhere. A little fairy dies when you say that.

I enjoy not giving so much of a fuck. I'm really happy in my life and things don't bother me as much as they used to. I think it'll all come out in the wash. We'll work it out. I feel I'm much more sanguine about things, especially as I've got such a crazy life with so many things going on. It's always this sort of mental schedule and trying to make it all work, but I just now think, “It'll be fine.” So that's a good thing about being older.

MH: What are you most curious about these days?

AC: Lots of things. I'm running a theater now and every day there are things I've got to deal with and talk about and find out about, and that's amazing. I joined TikTok today, so I decided to do that. I want to learn to play the bagpipes. I want to learn to type properly because, I mean, I use my computer, obviously, and I've written books and films, but I've never really properly learned to type. And I want to get better at Spanish, and I have a sort of trad wife fantasy of making gluten-free scones in my AGA, which is a kind of country stove.

AC: I don't really feel this age, but when I was 33, I moved to New York, and I feel like my life hasn't really changed that much since then. I still live in the same area. I still have a lot of the same friends. I do a lot of the same things. I have the same kind of life. I don't go out as much as I used to, but I love dancing still, and I would do that more if people didn't take photos of me all the time. Before mobile phone cameras, you didn't have to worry about being off your tits and dancing in a club with your chums. Now you do.

I'm obviously not 33. I don't look 33. But I feel like I'm as fit as I was when I was 33, kind of.

#4818. Rivian electric van spotted in Walmart+ livery, hinting at a fleet deal

A Rivian electric delivery van wrapped in Walmart+ branding was photographed on a car hauler on I-94 in northwest Indiana today. It’s the first public sign that Walmart could become Rivian’s next big van customer after Amazon.

Neither company has announced a deal. But Walmart’s last two electric van suppliers are out of the business, and Rivian is one of the few companies still building a purpose-built electric delivery van in the US.

Reddit user biggie_ballzzz posted the photo to r/RIVNstock this afternoon, asking if anyone had heard about a partnership. The van is strapped to a multi-car trailer between two Ford pickups, with a big “Walmart+” logo on the side and “Same day. Right to your door.” on the rear doors.

There’s no mistaking the vehicle. It’s Rivian’s Commercial Van, with the same tall body and red light bar wrapping around the rear that you see on Amazon Prime vans everywhere.

A few commenters suspected an AI image, but there’s no clear evidence. In fact, a second commenter then shared a photo of a van in the same livery parked in front of a Walmart Supercenter in Hammond, Indiana, about 30 miles to the west.

Rivian (RIVN) stock was up more than 3% this afternoon as the photo made the rounds, according to screenshots shared in the thread. That’s two days before Rivian reports its Q3 2026 results on Thursday, October 29.

Walmart has been trying to electrify last-mile delivery for years. Its supplier picks haven’t aged well.

In 2022, it signed up to buy 4,500 Canoo vans and put them to work on InHome deliveries. Canoo filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy in January 2025 and ceased operations.

The same year, Walmart reserved 5,000 BrightDrop vans from GM, and officially added them to its delivery fleet in late 2024. Then GM killed BrightDrop production at its CAMI plant in Ontario a year ago, with no plan to build the van anywhere else. BrightDrop was on pace for roughly 4,000 US sales in 2025, compared to more than 60,000 for GM’s gas-powered Express and Savana vans.

So Walmart is running two orphaned EV van platforms. And if it wants more purpose-built electric vans at scale, the list of US options is very short.

Amazon ordered 100,000 vans from Rivian, and its fleet has now passed 40,000 units on the road. But the deal came with an exclusivity period that ended in November 2023, and Rivian has struggled to land anything close to Amazon-scale since.

AT&T signed up for a pilot in late 2023, and HelloFresh came on board in 2025. In February 2025, Rivian opened van sales to any business, with the RCV 500 starting at $79,900 and the larger RCV 700 at $83,900. None of those customers moves the needle like Walmart would.

There’s also a charging angle. Walmart now operates its own 400 kW fast-charging network at 100 stores in 20 states, and its manager of retail charging, Wade Higgins, previously worked at Rivian, according to his bio on the board of Minnesota car-sharing nonprofit HOURCAR.

One van on a trailer isn’t a fleet order. Not yet, anyway. This could be a test unit for a pilot program, like the one AT&T announced in 2023. And since Rivian sells vans to any business now, Walmart could have simply bought a few to try them out.

So Walmart is running two orphaned EV van platforms. And if it wants more purpose-built electric vans at scale, the list of US options is very short.

Walmart also runs Ford E-Transit vans but I can't find recent numbers for how many

But the timing makes sense. Walmart bet on Canoo and GM, and both left it with vans nobody builds anymore. If you’re Walmart and you want to keep electrifying same-day delivery, Rivian is the obvious call. Its plant in Normal, Illinois, has already built tens of thousands of these vans, and the platform has been proven at scale by the one company Walmart is trying to beat on delivery.

That’s the awkward part. Walmart putting its brand on the same van as Amazon Prime is a bit funny, and it says a lot about how thin the electric van market has gotten in the US.

For Rivian, a Walmart deal would matter. The van business gives it volume in Normal while R2 ramps, and it badly needs proof that the van isn’t just an Amazon product. We’ll see if Rivian says anything on Thursday’s call. We wouldn’t bet on a massive order announcement, but a Walmart pilot wouldn’t surprise us one bit.

#4817. The 2027 Men’s Health Tech Awards

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

From smart swim goggles to self-cleaning vacuums.

DO YOU REALLY need an app for everything? Men’s Health’s Reviews Team spent the year trying gadgets that promise to make life easier, and often come with another login or an AI feature to figure out first. Resident tech guys—including Senior Gear Editor Ryan Brower, Fitness Editor Charles Thorp, and Senior Editor Brett Williams—have tried enough to know which ones are worth the trouble and your hard-earned dollars.

Their favorites make up this year’s Tech Awards, from swim goggles that show your pace in the lens to a massage gun that runs for up to four hours per charge and still fits in your gym bag. We also found time-saving gadgets like a robot vacuum that washes its own mop, so you can cross one more chore off your weekend list.

TVs that double as wall art are everywhere, but plenty come with gallery-worthy prices. Amazon’s 65-inch model gets you the look for less, with frame options to match your room and a matte screen that cuts glare. Alexa voice control is pretty great at this price: Just ask it to find a show or turn up the volume without reaching for the remote.

Figure out what’s costing you strokes without spending your round staring at your phone. This pocket-size tracker records shots without sensors attached to your clubs, then syncs with an app that breaks down your game. One MH editor used it to pinpoint the approach-shot distances he needed to practice. Expect occasional manual corrections after a round. The first year of membership is included; keeping those insights coming costs $200 annually after that.

A bargain given all that it does, the Xpress Lite features a durable-yet-lightweight frame and smooth-as-silk pedaling. The styling is a modern take on a cruiser, and the 500-watt motor barely makes a sound. With five pedal-assist modes, up to 45 miles of range, and assisted speeds up to 28 mph when configured for Class 3 riding, this e-bike slays.

This exoskeleton from Hypershell provides 1,000 watts of extra oomph, with 12 adaptive assist functions that respond to your movement. On a steep, rocky hike, one MH tester felt a noticeable boost lifting his legs uphill and steadier on the descent. Two included batteries offer roughly 18 to 20 miles apiece, depending on terrain, load, and how much assistance you use. You’ll still earn the view—just with a little help on the climb.

Mileseey Golf GeneSonic Pro Detachable GPS Speaker

A golf speaker? Oh yes. This one brings the party and useful course info to the back nine. A detachable handheld GPS comes loaded with more than 43,000 golf courses, so you can check distances before choosing your club. Meanwhile, the boisterous subwoofer gives your playlist some punch. Keep the music on the cart and take the GPS with you when it’s time to line up your shot.

Did you know you could wear a swim instructor as a pair of goggles? This pair shows your pace and elapsed time right in the lens, so you can check your splits without stopping at the wall. Add a Form Premium subscription for guided workouts and stroke coaching as you swim. The fit is comfortable, and the display takes little getting used to. We’re especially stoked to have a plan to follow instead of swimming the same laps.

Helly Hansen Atlas Infinity H2Flow Shell Jacket

Cold on the chairlift, yet sweating halfway down the run? This waterproof ski jacket pairs strategically placed insulation with vents that let you release excess heat. An insulated phone pocket helps protect your battery from the cold, and reinforced shoulders add durability where you carry your skis. The helmet-compatible hood and removable powder skirt help keep snow out when it really starts coming down.

Your commute and the school pickup don’t usually call for the same bike. This modular e-bike shape-shifts like a Transformer, switching from cruiser to cargo-hauler or kid-transporter without extra tools. Full suspension smooths out rough pavement, and the removable battery doubles as a power bank. It’s a splurge, but you get plenty of bang for your buck. The Performance edition offers assisted speeds up to 28 mph and, with the Large battery, up to 100 miles of range.

Oakley gives smart sunglasses a sporty look with a wraparound shape and bold tinted lenses. Capture photos and video from your point of view without pulling out your phone, and play your running playlist through built-in open-ear speakers. Pair them with a compatible Garmin watch or bike computer to ask for your pace or heart rate aloud. You can also overlay workout stats on photos and videos to share through Strava.

Our best fitness tracker for Android keeps the design minimalist, but packs plenty of useful training tools inside. Dual-frequency GPS helps track your route more accurately around tall buildings and trees. Running Coach recommends workouts based on your fitness level, and sleep coaching suggests habits to improve your nightly routine. Once set up with your phone, it records workouts on its own. Choose the LTE version with an active cellular plan to take calls without keeping your phone in your running shorts.

These workout earbuds stay put as you move through your sets, with four adjustable hook positions to help you find a comfortable fit. The open-ear design lets you hear someone asking to work in, and IP55 dust and water resistance helps them handle sweaty sessions. You get up to 8.5 hours of playback per charge, pretty impressive at this price.

Suji’s app-controlled blood-flow-restriction cuffs use personalized pressure settings to make lighter-load exercise more demanding. One MH editor found 20-lb curls plenty challenging and liked having the cuffs along for underwhelming hotel gyms. Guided workouts help you put them to use without guessing your way through a session. Check with your doctor or physical therapist before starting, especially when returning from injury or surgery.

Step on and grip the handle for estimates of body fat and muscle mass, including breakdowns for your arms, legs, and torso. The app charts changes over time to give your training more context. Treat those readings as estimates to track consistently, rather than a precise verdict on every pound gained or lost.

Keep your hands free and your attention on the trail. This lightweight headlamp adjusts its brightness and beam pattern to the light around you, so you spend less time fiddling with settings mid-run. A quick double tap delivers a six-second boost for checking the route ahead. The thin headband adjusts for a snug fit, and USB-C charging gets it ready for your next early start or after-dark hike.

This speaker brings plenty of sound for backyard hangs, plus lighting effects for when the sun goes down. Our testers cranked up bass-heavy tracks expecting it to struggle, but it held its own. Expect up to 20 hours of battery life with the lights off, with less runtime at higher volumes.

Set it on your desk when the office heat is cranked up, or use the included wristlet to bring it along on your next tropical vacation. A treadmill mount and other accessories are sold separately.

This electric toothbrush combines sweeping and vibrating motions, with settings you can fine-tune in the app. A pressure sensor warns you when you’re pressing too hard, and a two-minute timer keeps your routine on track. It gradually builds up to your chosen speed over three seconds to help keep toothpaste from splattering across the mirror.

A little helper during pollen season or when you share your space with a shedding pet.

#4816. BYD’s $10,000 EV blows a tire at nearly 90 mph — Watch what happens

BYD updated its lowest-priced electric car, the Seagull, which starts at around $10,000 in China, with a few extras, including a high-speed tire blowout system that stabilizes the vehicle at nearly 90 mph.

If the $10,000 price tag wasn’t enough, BYD is giving buyers even more reason to check out its entry-level electric hatch.

The Seagull is among BYD’s most popular vehicles, sold as the Dolphin Surf in Europe and the UK and as the Dolphin Mini in other global markets.

BYD launched the second-generation Seagull EV last week, starting at just 62,900 yuan, or about $9,500. That’s including BYD’s limited-time Super Trade-In incentive.

Regular prices start at 65,900 yuan ($9,900), which is still less than its predecessor. The first-generation Seagull EV started at 69,900 yuan ($10,500) without incentives, making it BYD’s most affordable purely electric vehicle in China.

For its second generation, the Seagull is bigger, more advanced, and adds a bit more luxury to the entry-level segment.

The new BYD Seagull is 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. That’s 425 mm longer and has a 150 mm longer wheelbase than the previous model.

Thanks to the added space, BYD’s electric hatch now offers room for five passengers, up from four seats that the first-gen Seagull had.

BYD added several new features with its latest tech, including a bigger 15.6″ infotainment screen with its DiLink 150 smart cockpit system and a “140 km/h high-speed tire blowout stability system” as standard.

To showcase how the tire blowout system works, BYD put the updated electric hatch to the test at full speed.

BYD’s general manager of the Ocean Series, Zhang Zhuo, shared a video of the second-generation Seagull EV handling the blowout at 140 km/h, or about 87 mph, like it’s nothing.

The high-speed tire-blowout system lets the Seagull stay in its lane until it comes to a complete stop. Pretty impressive for an entry-level vehicle.

As you can see in the video, the new version also has an available roof-mounted LiDAR. Buyers can upgrade to the optional DiPilot 300 system with BYD’s God’s Eye intelligent driving assistance. The ADAS system provides features like City Navigation on Autopilot (CNOA) and smart parking.

BYD added a few premium extras, including heating, ventilation, and a massage function to the front seats, plus ambient lighting, smart storage options, and a 50W wireless phone charger.

The new Seagull uses BYD’s Blade Batteries 2.0 and Flash Charging Technology. As such, the battery can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. A full recharge, or 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes. Even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it takes 12 minutes to charge from 20% to 97%.

It’s available with two LFP battery packs: 30.1 kWh and 39.2 kWh, providing CLTC ranges of 320 km (199 miles) and 420 km (261 miles), respectively.

To improve the ride quality and handling, BYD upgraded the rear suspension to a multi-link independent system.

The second-gen Seagull also switches to front-wheel-drive (FWD) with a more powerful 85 kW (114 hp) or 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from the 55 kW (75 hp) that its predecessor offered.

BYD’s new Seagull is available in five variants, priced from 65,900 yuan to 99,900 yuan ($9,900 to $15,000), without a trade-in.

After launching the second-gen Seagull in China, BYD is expected to introduce the updated version overseas. It will likely be the second-generation Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.

#4815. How to Use the Deficit Deadlift to Produce More Power on Your Pulls

Increasing your deadlift's range of motion can help you build strength through the toughest part of the lift.

LITTLE CHANGES CAN yield big results. If you’re working to set new strength standards and push through weight room plateaus, movements like the deficit deadlift stand as testament to that sentiment. The exercise is identical to the traditional barbell deadlift, with one key distinction: You stand on a slightly elevated surface—we're talking just a couple of inches—as you pull the weight off the floor.

There's a good chance you haven't tried this variation before. It's more popular among strength athletes, like powerlifters and strongmen, who toil over every minute detail of their deadlift technique to gain a competitive edge. But just because you haven't done it doesn't mean you shouldn't. Whether you're looking to shake up your routine or address a specific weakness in your deadlift, this simple adjustment is worth trying. Here's what you need to know.

DEFICIT DEADLIFTS EXTEND the range of motion of the pull by the height of whatever you're standing on, usually an inch or two, making the lift more demanding. Athletes who train for strength sports typically add deficit deadlifts to their programs when they're having trouble pulling heavier weights off the floor.

Say you can deadlift 315 pounds, but can't budge 335. You might be struggling to produce enough force during the initial pull. By standing on an elevated surface, you're forcing the muscles responsible for getting the bar moving—primarily your glutes and quads with a little help from your hamstrings and lower back—to work through a greater range of motion.

The extra demand on these muscles “can potentiate more muscle growth and greater strength—especially grip strength,” says Lee Boyce, a Toronto-based personal trainer, college professor, and owner of Boyce Training Systems. “Reaching down further than normal to pick up a bar also means more quadriceps activity, due to the greater knee bend that's required to do so. Transitioning back to a standard deadlift after a phase of deficit work can give the normal stuff the chance to feel ‘easy’ by comparison.”

This concept isn’t simply theoretical. A small study of 20 experienced lifters compared conventional deadlifts, deficit deadlifts, and rack pulls (which have you lifting a heavier weight than you can deadlift over a smaller range of motion). Researchers found more quad and glute activation during deficit deadlifts. The study measured only muscle engagement, not whether that engagement leads to greater muscle growth. Still, what’s clear is this: deficit deadlifts offer another way to challenge your lower body without introducing an entirely different movement.

Boyce says deficit deadlifts can also be a good fit for shorter lifters who want a longer pulling range. “Being shorter means the bar will ‘start’ higher up the leg, making for a shorter range of motion and a pull that may not be as fulfilling,” he explains. “Standing on a platform or a couple of plates can fix this problem.”

That won’t work for everyone, though, especially beginners. Celebrity trainer Don Saladino likes deficit deadlifts but says the added mobility demands mean they're not a good fit for every lifter. “I work with plenty of people who lack the mobility or control to deadlift properly from the floor, and so why would I increase their range of motion?” he shared in an October 20 Instagram post. “In many cases, I’m doing the opposite. I’m elevating the bar to help them achieve a stronger, more controlled starting position.”

Deficit deadlifts demand more mobility in your hips and ankles since you're reaching farther down to grab the bar. If you're excessively rounding your lower back to get into the starting position or your hips shoot up before the bar leaves the floor, you need to address those form issues before diving into deficit deadlifts. Try lifting from a smaller deficit or skip the exercise altogether. Dedicated hip mobility work may help you get there, but deficit deadlifts aren't a must-do exercise. There are plenty of deadlift variations to choose from, and the best one is the one that suits your abilities and training goals.

THE DEFICIT DEADLIFT is more of a modification than a distinct exercise. The instructions below focus on the barbell version, but you can perform just about any type of deadlift from a deficit, including dumbbell deadlifts, kettlebell deadlifts, and trap bar deadlifts. Check out the clip below, then follow the exercise cues.

Step 1: First, establish an elevated surface to stand on. Some strength gyms have dedicated platforms for deficit deadlifts. Make sure the surface is stable and large enough to accommodate your stance.

Step 2: Stand on the elevated surface in front of a loaded barbell, positioning the bar over the middle of your feet. Grab the bar with an overhand grip, just outside your legs. Then, bend your knees until they're next to your arms—not jutting past them or leaving a gap between your knees and arms when viewed from the side. This should naturally put your hips in a good starting position.

Step 3: Take a deep breath into your abdomen and brace your core as if you're preparing to take a punch. Keeping your arms extended, lift your chest as though you're showing off the logo on your shirt. Then, drive through your feet to pull the barbell off the floor.

Step 4: Keep the barbell as close to your legs as possible as you pull it up your shins and thighs. The bar may lightly brush against your legs, but that's okay. Keeping the weight close to your body reduces the demand on your lower back and puts you in a more efficient pulling position.

Step 5: Once you're standing tall with your hips and knees fully extended, reverse the movement by pushing your hips back and bending your knees to lower the barbell to the floor under control.

THE DEFICIT DEADLIFT is still a deadlift, so your pulling techniques shouldn’t change much. Those extra inches, though, will alter your form a bit, so it’s crucial to understand the potential pitfalls you may encounter when trying this subtly different deadlift variation.

An extra inch or two of range doesn't seem like much, but it changes the mechanics of your deadlift and places greater demands on your lower body muscles. Trying to lift the same weights you use for traditional deadlifts may compromise your form, especially if you're not accustomed to the increased range of motion. Start lighter and work your way up.

The first time you program deficit deadlifts, think of starting with 75-80% of your standard working weight. So if you do three hard sets of five reps with 275 pounds for standard deadlifts, you’d start around 205 or 225 pounds for your first deficit deadlift session. Your glutes and hammies will still get plenty of stimulus, and the weight will be light enough for you to handle through the extended range of motion.

It's common to see folks tap the weight on the floor and bounce it into their next deadlift rep (called a touch-and-go rep). At the start of your deficit deadlift programming, don’t do this. Remember that you’re doing deficit deadlifts to strengthen your initial pull from the floor, so you'll get more out of the exercise by treating every rep as a single rep.

After you lower the barbell to the ground, reset your hips, re-tighten your core, and pull the weight as if you’re trying for a one-rep max. You can eventually train deficit deadlifts with touch-and-go mechanics. But first, master the move as a true deadlift.

If you're new to deficit deadlifts, start with a shorter elevation of around an inch. Stick with that height for a few weeks to see how it affects your form and how comfortable you feel pulling from a deeper position. If you can maintain your usual deadlift mechanics, you can experiment with adding another half inch to an inch.

Some powerlifters pull from deficits of two to four inches, sometimes even higher. You don't need to go to those extremes. (“I wouldn’t recommend exceeding six inches,” Boyce adds.) For most lifters, one to two inches is plenty to make the movement more challenging. Instead of continually increasing the height, focus on progressively overloading your deficit deadlift by gradually adding more reps or weight as you get stronger.

YOU CAN USE the deficit deadlift either as a primary strength exercise or as an accessory to your regularly scheduled deadlift regimen. Because they’re more demanding, beginners should start with two to three sets of three to five reps once per week. You can do them after your main deadlift work, if you don’t feel too fatigued, or on a different training day.

“Deficit work is best done in sets of under six reps due to the neural demands of pulling heavy weight beyond the regular range of motion,” Boyce says. “Treating them as a typical strength training exercise would be the smart call here.”

If you’re a more experienced deadlifter, you can sub them in as your primary pulling exercise for a training block (typically four to six weeks). Some competitive powerlifters even work up to a heavy set of one to three reps—but unless you’re training for maximal strength, you don’t need to lift this heavy for deficit deadlifts. Start lighter, get comfortable with the range of motion, and gradually add weight over time.

#4814. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Your hub for heart health management, insights, and solutions

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This new study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

This was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

The researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

They measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

The researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

Among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

When the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is important to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

These findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” said Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

“Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd said.

Judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more important to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

She said that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is important to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

“I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” said Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”

#4813. Renewables to reach 40% of total generating capacity, beat gas within a year – EIA

Over the coming year, renewables’ share of total generating capacity will grow from 37.7% to 40.4%, surpassing that of natural gas and outstripping nuclear capacity fivefold, according to new data released by the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) and reviewed by the SUN DAY Campaign.

According to the EIA’s latest “Electric Power Monthly” report (with data through August 31, 2026), renewably generated electricity during the first two-thirds of 2026 was 10.2% greater year over year. The growth was led by utility-scale [>1 MW] solar (up 20.0%), small-scale solar (up 12.0%), wind (up 7.8%), hydropower (up 4.2%), and geothermal (up 3.8%).

From January to August 2026, wind produced 333,367 gigawatt-hours (GWh) – 10.6% of total US electrical generation – while utility-scale and small-scale solar combined produced 329,119 GWh (10.5%), hydropower produced 180,940 GWh (5.7%), biomass produced 29,917 GWh (1.0%), and geothermal produced 10,766 GWh (0.34%).

By comparison, the electrical output of US natural gas and nuclear power plants grew more slowly – by just 2.6% and 1.3%, respectively. Electricity produced by US coal plants fell by 8.7%.

During the first eight months of 2026, the combination of wind and solar, including small-scale solar, accounted for almost 21.1% of domestic electricity production, with wind at 10.6% and solar at nearly 10.5%.

During the first two-thirds of this year, wind and solar combined produced 44.4% more electricity than coal and 24.8% more than nuclear.

Through the end of August, the mix of all renewables, including biomass, accounted for 28.1% of total US electrical generation – up from 26.2% a year earlier.

Between September 1, 2025, and August 31, 2026, the installed capacity of utility-scale solar increased by 27,141.7 MW, while that of small-scale solar and wind grew by 6,526.1 MW and 9,979.1 MW (including 800 MW of offshore wind), respectively. The combined capacity of all renewable energy sources, including hydropower, biomass, and geothermal, expanded by 43,497.9 MW.

In addition, utility-scale battery energy storage capacity increased by 17,586.9 MW.

By comparison, coal capacity fell by 2,703.4 MW, while nuclear capacity remained unchanged. However, natural gas capacity rose by 5,316.0 MW. Combined, net new nuclear and fossil fuel capacity totaled just 2,612.6 MW.

Thus, renewable energy’s capacity expansion was nearly 17 times greater than the net growth of fossil fuels and nuclear power combined.

The EIA projects that the rapid growth of renewables over the past year will accelerate in the coming year.

As of September 1, 2026, renewable energy’s share of total US utility-scale generating capacity was 34.5%. EIA projects this to grow to 37.3% by August 31, 2027. Utility-scale solar will add 44,603.1 MW, thereby expanding its share from 13.4% to 16.5%, while wind will grow by 8,312.3 MW (including 3,355.0 MW of offshore wind), increasing from 13.4% to 13.5%. The mix of other renewables (hydropower, biomass, and geothermal) will add 201.9 MW.

The combined net capacity growth of all utility-scale renewable energy sources over the 12-month period (53,117.3 MW) is almost 44% higher than that added over the previous 12 months (36,971.8 MW). It would bring renewables’ share of total US utility-scale generating capacity up to 37.3%.

Meanwhile, EIA projects no new nuclear generating capacity and a net decline of 1,997.0 MW in fossil fuel capacity.

The figures cited above don’t include small-scale solar. The estimated capacity of small-scale solar systems grew by 6,526.1 MW during the last year, bringing its total to 63,192.6 MW. EIA does not provide a forecast for small-scale solar capacity growth over the next 12 months, but the SUN DAY Campaign assumes it will roughly equal the 6,400 MW added on average over each of the past five years. Therefore, it is conservatively assumed that an additional 6,000 MW or more will come online in the coming year.

If small-scale solar increases by approximately 6,000 MW by September 1, 2027, it will bring renewable energy’s installed capacity to about 550,000 MW. By comparison, natural gas’ projected generating capacity would total 518,312.8 MW.

Solar power’s share alone would be more than one-fifth (20.7%) of total US generating capacity.

EIA foresees battery energy storage adding another 23,656.2 MW by September 1, 2027 – an increase of 43.7%, bringing the total up to 77,753.2 MW.

Thus, the combination of utility-scale renewable energy sources and battery energy storage will provide 76,773.5 MW of new clean energy capacity by late summer 2027. With the inclusion of small-scale solar, that figure could rise to 82.8 GW of new generating capacity.

Google CAISO to see what percent of the California grid is supplied by renewable energy on each and every day, typically more than 70% and often 100%., And they have 16 GW of battery storage, providing renewable electricity 24 seven to the California electrical grid.

“Each new issue of EIA’s ‘Electric Power Monthly’ reinforces the theme that the growth of solar, wind, and battery storage has become unstoppable,” noted the SUN DAY Campaign’s executive director Ken Bossong. “Meanwhile, the share of the nation’s electrical generation and generating capacity provided by fossil fuels and nuclear continues to shrink.”

#4812. Steve Buscemi’s Secret to Stealing a Scene

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

“My job is to come in and pretend like it’s my movie!”

I’M LOOKING RIGHT into Steve Buscemi’s eyes, which on this early October morning happen to sit behind a pair of black-framed glasses, stylishly matching the collared shirt and jacket he’s wearing. Looking into Buscemi’s eyes is kinda like looking at the sun—even when he isn’t quite as animated as some of the characters he plays, his demeanor comes across warm and thoughtful. The 68-year-old is a New York native, and it’s easy to picture an alternate world where he’s the neighbor who always greets you in the hallway—instead of a face you’ve seen in a number of classic movies and shows that probably approaches triple digits.

Much like the sun, sometimes Buscemi’s eyes—and the rest of him—are at their strongest when doled out in limited quantities, adding an indescribable excellence to a movie or show in need of some extra oomph.

His latest role comes in Wild Horse Nine, a darkly comedic thriller from writer/director Martin McDonagh, the Oscar-winning Irish filmmaker behind movies like In Bruges and The Banshees of Inisherin. The film follows a pair of longtime friends and CIA officers, Chris (John Malkovich) and Lee (Sam Rockwell), in 1973 as they visit Easter Island in Chile, just ahead of the infamous coup d’état. Chris, who is terminally ill, is essentially being put out to pasture by the agency, and wants to take a visit from their station in Santiago, and Lee joins him. Buscemi plays a supporting role, popping up throughout its runtime as MJ, the spectacularly dressed and morally dubious boss to our lead duo.

Buscemi has played lead roles before, including, most notably, in HBO’s hit series Boardwalk Empire, for which he won a Golden Globe and was nominated for two Emmys. But it’s those supporting roles—in everything from blockbusters like Con Air to classics like Reservoir Dogs and The Big Lebowski to cameos in Adam Sandler movies—that have made him iconic, and it’s those kinds of movies where people see him put some of his best work on display. How, then, does he so regularly make a character like MJ feel lived-in and three-dimensional in a movie that mostly follows Chris and Lee?

“I don’t really worry about what their story is,” he explains with a laugh. “You know? My job is to come in and pretend like it’s my movie!”

He explains that he read Frank Capra’s autobiography, The Name Above the Title, where the It’s a Wonderful Life director makes it clear that he considers every character in one of his films to be worthy of their own standalone narrative. “The thing I care about most is the part I’m playing… it doesn’t matter how big it is,” he says. “But are they important to the story? It doesn’t matter how much screen time he has.”

It’s a busy season for Buscemi, who’s not only in Wild Horse Nine, but also plays a key supporting role alongside his old friend (and fellow Coen brothers collaborator) John Turturro in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York. As the former film hits theaters and with the latter already out, Buscemi spoke to Men’s Health about locking in on his roles, close friendships, and memories with the cast of The Big Lebowski.

MEN’S HEALTH: What draws you to a project?

STEVE BUSCEMI: I mean, I like compelling characters. I like ensemble films and ensemble casts. I like good writing and good directing, and with Martin you get that in one package. Knowing it was a Martin McDonagh script, already I’m saying yes before I even read the script, practically. I’m reading it going, [Laughs] I hope I love this as much as I think I’m going to love it. And I did.

MH: Is there any learning curve when you’re working with someone new, who has such a specific vision of what he wants?

SB: There was a bit of nervousness, only because I wanted to do a good job. I wanted to do my best. I did have the advantage of getting to hang out with him in Venice when Banshees of Inisherin was there, four years ago. And we really got on really well. We laughed a lot together, and so that put me at ease, knowing that he was a gentle soul, and seemed like he was going to be very open and collaborative. But I was still just nervous because, you know, the material is just so high up there, and knowing it was going to be John, and Sam… you never want to be the weak link [Laughs]. I just wanted to do my best.

MH: Speaking of John and Sam, you guys have this very lived-in dynamic—did you have to work ahead of time to achieve that?

SB: I’ve known Sam for like 35 years. I don’t always get to see him, but whenever I do, we just kind of fall back to that easiness of, we just really like each other and want to know what we’re up to. We have a lot of mutual friends, and people we’ve worked with. I don’t know John as well, but I have worked with him, and naturally, the scene we did in the office, that’s the only scene I have with John, we filmed that later. So, I got to hang out with him quite a bit when we were in Rapa Nui, on Easter Island. We were all staying at the same resort, so it was very easy to run into each other. And everything about our relationship—not that I have such a big relationship with John—but I’ve known him for a long time, I really respect him, I admire him, and I think I would be very intimidated if I were to direct him. So imagining that I would be his boss [laughs], it’s like, you want his respect, but if he doesn’t give it to you, how crushing that would be? I think that really served my character well.

MH: Is there any sort of mental hurdle to that? Like, locking in and being like ‘I am John Malkovich’s boss.”

SB: You just dive in. The material is so good, and John is so nice. He’s not an actor that will play games with you on set, or try and intimidate you. He’s just so open and easy to work with. I love that, because then you can really feel like ‘Oh, if I go at him hard, it’s OK.’ Or if he goes at me hard, it’s fine. We’re not going to take it personally.

MH: Does shooting on location in Chile come with a different experience?

SB: In Santiago, we were shooting in the square where the coup happened. So, that was very powerful just to imagine that this is where those real events happened. Then shooting on Easter Island, Rapa Nui… that’s a magical place. The horses really do run wild, and the dogs run wild, and there’s chickens and cows, and the Moai are incredible, and the history there. Like I said, we were all staying in the same resort, so it was just all about the work. There weren’t any real distractions. Everywhere you look informed the work that we were doing.

MH: Did you do any kind of research ahead of time?

SB: I asked Martin, “What should I be reading?” and he suggested this one book on the CIA that was very… I don’t know, it got very in the weeds, and the main gist of it—I couldn’t even finish it because it was just so disheartening to know what the CIA had been up to. But there’s a lot of big egos, and maybe that was the main thing I took away from it. I think MJ is very ambitious, and I love the outfits that he wore. That was one thing that really informed me—like, OK, this guy thinks a lot of himself. That’s good. I think I had first envisioned him as more of a bureaucrat in simple suits. So, I like that about the character, and I liked that he had that other dimension to him, where he had that coping mechanism. That, to me, made him very human.

MH: Is it fun to bounce back and forth between genres?

SB: As an actor, I’ve always wanted to sort of be able to do it all, and not be confined to any one genre. When I first started out, I did a lot of independent films, which I loved. It was in the late ’80s and ’90s, and I think that was a time when independent film was really coming into its own. But I never wanted to just be known as, like, “the independent film guy.” I wanted to do other things. I wanted to work in studio movies, comedies, TV—and I feel very lucky that I’ve been able to explore and get work in all these different types of films, and I don’t feel constricted to be any one way or to do any one thing.

MH: Does that inform how you approach and play your latest roles?

SB: I don’t know that it informs how I would do it, but I think, certainly, maybe the work that Martin has seen me do in the past, like with the Coen brothers, or Quentin, or Boardwalk, made him think I was right for this character. Whatever the reason he thought of me, I’m happy [laughs].

MH: Was there any kind of bump in the road along the way on Wild Horse Nine?

SB: Not really a bump in the road, but just wanting to do my best. I have a monologue at the end, where I’m telling Sam’s character the way things are going to go, and the way things are, and I knew that was an important part of the story, and part of MJ’s character. And you just want to get it right. These days, I have to spend more time on the script, and learning the lines, and getting it right, than when I was younger, when I used to just be able to pick things up very quickly. It takes more work now, but it’s OK [laughs].

MH: At the end of the day, Wild Horse Nine is a story of close friendship between these two guys who would do anything for each other. Is there anyone in the industry who’s like that for you?

SB: I have a very old friend, Mark Boone Junior, and we used to write and perform our own theater pieces, and I feel like it was with him that I learned a lot about being an actor. I also learned how to write, because he and I used to write our own shows, and also, by default, we would direct ourselves. So, that was the beginning of me directing. I feel like I owe a lot to him, and that time in my life. We live on different coasts and we don’t see each other a lot, but whenever we do, we just always fall back into that ease of friendship. He’s somebody I would do anything for, or anything that he asked of me.

MH: I have to end with a question about The Big Lebowski, which is my favorite movie of all time. Because not only have I just seen you in Wild Horse Nine, but I just saw John Goodman in Digger, and you’re also in Only Living Pickpocket in New York with John Turturro. What kind of relationship do you all have these days?

SB: I was very happy to work with John Turturro on Pickpocket, because I hadn’t worked with him in years and years. We know each other—I don’t live in Brooklyn anymore, but we used to live in the same neighborhood. I see him around town, or at screenings, or festivals. And so it was so satisfying and gratifying to be able to do a movie with him in New York.

Goodman, I haven’t seen in a while, but a few years ago, I don’t know what anniversary it was of The Big Lebowski, but me, John, and Jeff Bridges sat down for an interview, and then we had dinner afterwards, and it was just… I don’t even think we hung out that much during the making of the movie. But that dinner, that night, we just had the best time. And we were looking at each other, going, ‘Why didn’t we do this while we were making the movie?’ [Laughs] But that’s the nature of it—you know, we were filming in L.A., and when you’re filming in your home town, I mean, I don’t live there, but it’s such a spread out town. You do the work, and then you go off and do other things. That’s what I loved about shooting in Rapa Nui—we were just all there, and so we not only had the great memory of making the movie, but also hanging out together and having dinners, and seeing each other at breakfast.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#4811. How to Find the Optimal Romantic Partner

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 7, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

Choosing an optimal romantic partner is complex. We should consider the many factors and potential partners. Two distinctions are particularly important. The first is between the best person and the most compatible partner. The second is between dealbreakers (traits we seek to avoid) and dealmakers (traits we actively seek). The first distinction concerns the kind of person we are looking for; the second concerns the specific positive and negative traits we consider important. Both distinctions matter when choosing a partner wisely.

"If I had to dream up the perfect woman, she wouldn't even come close to you." — Boy Meets World

Potential partners are abundant in the romantic marketplace. We can assess their overall romantic value along two major dimensions: a nonrelational scale and a relational scale.

The nonrelational scale measures the value of traits considered independently of any particular relationship. These may include attractiveness, wisdom, intelligence, and kindness. This assessment has two advantages: It is relatively easy to assess, and people are likely to agree broadly about the value of such traits. By contrast, the relational scale measures a person's suitability within a specific relationship. It depends not only on each individual's characteristics, but also on the unique connection between them and their personal and environmental circumstances. Consequently, relational suitability is much more difficult to assess.

Consider long-term relationships. Should you marry an intelligent person? In general, intelligence is highly desirable. However, compatibility complicates the picture. A very large gap between partners' intellectual abilities may reduce their relational suitability. Similar considerations apply to many other traits and accomplishments. In enduring love, compatibility often matters more than excellence considered in isolation.

"Love thy neighbor. And if he happens to be tall, debonair, and devastating, it will be that much easier." — Mae West

"The one thing that is always a dealbreaker is a lack of physical attractiveness. Even the best personality in the world cannot seem to overcome that hurdle." — A man

Romantic search involves more than assessing overall value and compatibility. It also entails identifying specific virtues and flaws. Traits that discourage a relationship are commonly called dealbreakers. Examples include hostility, arrogance, abusiveness, excessive clinginess, poor hygiene, lack of ambition, and physical unattractiveness. Traits that encourage a relationship are known as dealmakers. Typical examples include intelligence, kindness, warmth, humor, physical attractiveness, social status, and financial stability. Everyone has strengths and weaknesses; romantic decisions depend heavily on the importance we assign to different dealmakers and dealbreakers.

Research consistently indicates that, when evaluating potential partners, people tend to weigh negative traits more heavily than positive ones. This finding reflects a broader psychological tendency: negative experiences generally affect us more strongly than positive ones. A positive characteristic may enrich our lives, but a serious negative characteristic can undermine an entire relationship (Ben-Ze’ev, A., 2019).

Dealbreakers are particularly influential when people consider long-term committed relationships rather than brief sexual encounters. Nevertheless, evolutionary pressures have likely shaped mate preferences to remain sensitive to both short-term and long-term mating strategies. Research further suggests that women are generally less tolerant of undesirable traits and more likely than men to classify various characteristics as dealbreakers in a mate-selection context (Csajbók and Berkics, 2022; Jonason and colleagues, 2015, 2022).

A practical strategy is to identify approximately five dealmakers and five dealbreakers that matter most to you. When most of your desired dealmakers are present, you have good reasons to pursue a relationship; when several significant dealbreakers are present, you may justify reconsidering it. Of course, romantic life rarely follows rigid rules. A relationship may flourish even when a partner possesses only some of the desired dealmakers or exhibits one or two dealbreakers. A lot depends on personal circumstances, individual priorities, and the severity of undesirable traits.

"I never promised you a rose garden. Along with the sunshine, there's got to be a little rain sometime." — Lynn Anderson

Finding an optimal long-term romantic partner requires focusing primarily on compatibility and avoiding serious dealbreakers. This does not mean ignoring positive attributes. Rather, the first step is to identify and avoid major obstacles to a healthy relationship. Once these obstacles fade, partners can build a harmonious and flourishing romantic bond through their strengths, shared values, and mutual commitment.

Ben-Ze’ev, A. (2019). The arc of love: How our romantic lives change over time. University of Chicago Press.

Csajbók, Z., & Berkics, M. (2022). Seven deadly sins of potential romantic partners: The dealbreakers of mate choice. Personality and Individual Differences, 186, 111334.‏

Jonason, P. K., et. al. (2015). Relationship dealbreakers: Traits people avoid in potential mates. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 41, 1697-1711.

Jonason, P. K., White, K. P., Lowder, A. H., & Al-Shawaf, L. (2022). To see or not to see (again): Dealbreakers and dealmakers in relation to social inclusion. Frontiers in Psychology, 13, 1019272.

#4810. A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” said study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The new review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

Laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

“Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep issues related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

“A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein said. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein said.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

“For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein said. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”

Sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

“I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein said. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”

#4808. Bosch’s popular e-bike motor just got upgraded with more power and less weight

Bosch has unveiled the latest generation of its popular Active Line Plus electric bicycle motor, bringing more power, less weight, and a significantly smaller footprint to one of the company’s most widely used drive systems.

The new motor is designed primarily for everyday riders, including commuters, recreational cyclists, and those who want a comfortable e-bike that can handle everything from city streets to weekend trail rides.

And while it isn’t Bosch’s most powerful motor, the upgrades are fairly substantial.

The new Active Line Plus now produces up to 600 watts of peak power and 60 Nm of torque, along with a maximum pedal assistance level of 340%. That’s enough to give riders a healthy boost when accelerating away from traffic lights or climbing hills, without necessarily turning their everyday commuter into an overpowered mountain bike.

Like its predecessor, the motor is designed for Class 1 electric bicycles in the US, providing pedal assistance up to 20 mph (32 km/h) without a throttle.

Remember, the Active Line motor is the drive system model that many e-bike companies use for their modestly performing e-bikes. It gives good power and control, combined with all the tech we’ve come to expect from Bosch, but it isn’t the motor e-bike makers use when they need an electric mountain bike to scale a steep mountainous trail.

Perhaps even more interesting than the increased power is what Bosch has done to the motor’s physical design.

The company developed a new two-stage gearbox that helps reduce the motor’s overall volume by 17% while shaving approximately 1.1 lb (0.5 kg) off its weight.

The new drive unit now tips the scales at around 6 lb (2.7 kg), making it easier for bicycle manufacturers to integrate into slimmer, more traditional-looking frames.

Bosch also says the new gearbox uses specially machined gears to make the motor virtually silent, while updated sensors and software provide smoother, more natural-feeling pedal assistance.

That’s particularly important for a motor like the Active Line Plus, where riders are often looking for an experience that feels like riding a regular bicycle, just with a bit of extra help.

The motor also supports Bosch’s eShift electronic shifting system, which can automatically manage gear changes for riders who prefer to focus on pedaling instead of shifting.

Bosch has additionally improved the motor’s sealing and bearings for better all-weather durability. The housing uses approximately 40% recycled aluminum, helping reduce the carbon footprint of its production.

Trek will be the first North American bicycle brand to introduce the new Active Line Plus motor, installing it on the company’s Marlin+ electric bike.

Bosch also announced several other additions to its e-bike ecosystem, including a new compact LED Controller that’s 65% smaller than its predecessor, an updated ConnectModule with Bluetooth-based theft tracking, and a new 720 Wh PowerTube battery weighing just 8.6 lb (3.9 kg).

There’s also a new Intuvia 200 display, offering a 2.4-inch grayscale screen for riders who prefer a traditional handlebar-mounted display.

While high-performance e-bike motors tend to grab the headlines with increasingly outrageous torque figures, there’s something to be said for improvements to the more practical end of the market – something for the riders looking for convenient and effective transportation instead of peak performance figures.

For the average commuter or recreational rider, a quieter, lighter motor with plenty of usable power is likely to make a bigger difference than squeezing another few dozen Newton-meters out of an already powerful drive system.

And with Bosch’s extensive network of bicycle manufacturing partners, we can expect to see this updated motor making its way into plenty of new electric bikes.
