#4790. Is Yeti’s $200 Camp Blanket Worth It? I Tested It Out for Months to Find Out.

Hint: It low-key might be one of Yeti’s best products.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

YETI IS KNOWN to drop a lot of product. The Austin-based brand emerged as a key player in the cooler category and has since grown immensely, putting out everything from fleeces to outdoor furniture.

The Lowlands Blanket, an durable outdoor blanket, might be a piece that gets overlooked in the brand’s offering. The original came out a few years back but Yeti has added some new colors as well as improvements like the diamond-stitched pattern. It’s waterproof, claims to repel dirt and pet hair, and comes in a host of core and seasonal colors (not to mention two different sizes). As an all-purpose, throw-kind of blanket, it’s meant to be put to use pretty much anywhere, from the back of your car or atop some cold bleachers at the soccer game to the campsite or picnic at the beach or state park.

Do you need one though? That all depends. The $200 blanket proved quite capable during testing, packing down nicely and drying at speed. There are pros and cons to the thing, and it really depends on the lifestyle you’re trying to cater to, not to mention the elements you might be operating under.

While we were sitting on a regular-sized Lowlands Blanket during the summer months (quite literally), packing it to a few outdoor concerts and park picnics, we mostly waited patiently for fall. We wanted to really assess the burly, insulated build of the thing and its waterproofness. We spent several weeks with the blanket in the back of the car, at the ready for everything from dog naps and post-paddle warmups to hangouts near the wet soccer field or full-fledged fall camping trips.

Right out of the gate, this is easily one of the most comfortable outdoor blankets we’ve tested in recent history. Down blankets can offer a similar level of sensory joy but the softness of the topside of this blanket feels like something you’d get draped over the best chair in a ski lodge, right in front of the great room fire. It’s mildly fuzzy on one side and more coarse and rugged on the other.

The seasonal colors really pop and add some flavor while the two sizes of the blanket are actually quite distinct and useful in their own ways. The smaller, about 28-in. by 38-in., is about the size of a dog bed and is (surprise) best for pets—setting up a dry sitting spot for one, or thawing wipe downs after playing in the snow. It does not come with a carrying case but rolls up plenty small and doesn’t necessitate one. The larger (the one we tested), measuring 55-in. by 78-in., is more like a bed topper, great for picnics, topping your camp bed, or just wearing around in the cold.

The corner loops are a nice touch for securing the blanket in blustery conditions and can also be used for hanging or tying down valuables. We even tried hanging it up and utilizing it as a temporary wind barrier during outings that involved occasional sideways rain. We found that it worked well as a barrier during offseason camping trips. In other words, as a comforter of sorts to protect you from dirt or the elements while keeping your base-layers or sheets beneath dry.

Cleaning the thing is pretty simple, whether that be a quick wipe-down to address grass stains and mud or a full machine wash after a weekend camping in the woods. One of the blanket’s biggest merits is its thickness, offering more depth than most at close to a half-inch. You can genuinely feel it too. Often, when you throw a packable blanket atop the grass or the sand at the beach you’re banking on the inherent softness of that natural surface and not getting much else. Not so with the Yeti, as it does afford a true layer of added comfort, one that can easily eat up contours in uneven surfaces or small rocks and sticks.

Yeti tends to follow the go big or go home philosophy, which we’re used to at this point and oftentimes suits the product and its intentions well. At nearly six pounds, it’s admittedly a bit heavy for a blanket. But you can feel instantly where all that weight is going (the ample insulation and reinforced exterior). The weight is not a huge deal, especially if you utilize the packing bag that it comes with, which you can grab by hand or sling over your shoulder. It’s more noticeable if you’re just carrying it about unfolded or rearranging that picnic spread. But, because it translates to more comfort and durability, we’re all for it. Just keep it in mind for towing purposes if you’re looking for something to pack along on a hike, you can find something far lighter.

The internet has alerted us to the possibility of mold if not dried off properly or machine-washed fairly often. While we didn’t experience that, the blanket is thicker and seemingly takes on odors a bit more than some. What’s perhaps more of an issue is the noise, which is only relatively louder than, say, a puffy blanket, which tends to offer a more whispered kind of sound when moving about beneath it. This is probably only a real issue for sensitive sleepers.

For do-it-all blankets built for the outdoors, there are a few alternatives. Rumpl has a line of nimble options that often come in cool patterns. The price is right but you’re generally getting either a mat or a puffy (although you can certainly pair the two up for more waterproofness). They’re billed as weather-resistant and while they look great and feel like snuggling into a zipped sleeping bag, they don’t quite have the waterproof build and toughness of Yeti. However, if you’re after a high warmth-to-weight ratio, it’s tough to go wrong here. Nomadix makes another quality option, a puffer blanket that packs more tightly than most, weighs just two pounds, and is even made with a bunch of recycled material. Yet, if you’re going to be dealing with more than wet grass (e.g. snow) or plan to be in more than low-level precipitation, you’ll want something more substantial.

White Duck Outdoors makes a solid one too in the Trailside Blanket, which comes in under $100, weighs just three pounds, has a streamlined layer of insulation, and smart magnetic closures for when you want to wear it. While a lot of Pendleton’s blankets are form over function, the Oregon brand does make a nice all-weather option in the Roll-Up Blanket, priced comparably to the new Yeti. It does come armed with a weather-resistant nylon side and a soft wool side to hang out on.

For an all-purpose outdoor blanket that can take you from the snowy slopes to the trail and pretty much everywhere in between, this is a tough one to beat. It’s more durable than many we’ve tested, offers more comfort by way of added depth and nicely-stitched insulation, and even fends off pet hair swimmingly. While a great accompaniment to camping adventures, the Lowlands Blanket is also great for elevating the outdoor music festival, throwing atop a damp yard, or lugging to the tailgater (especially in the fall and winter).

This regular size is $200, a fair chunk of change (the small version is $75). And while that’s not cheap, it simply outdoes just about every other blanket in its class. You may not need a heavier, weatherproof blanket if you mostly spend time car camping. But if you want a burly blanket that’s not afraid of the terrain or weather, this one’s for you. Offseason campers are wise to consider it, as are diehard sports fans who like to show up for their team.

#4789. Why We Hug and What Makes an Embrace Memorable?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 7, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

Can you remember the last time you hugged someone?

Most people hug quite a lot over their lifetime (Ocklenburg, 2024). Many hugs are mundane, like a quick one when greeting or goodbye. But occasionally, we may experience a hug that is emotionally more significant than a quick hi. The first time someone hugs the love of their life, or the last time someone hugs their mum before she dies, may be hugs some people remember for the rest of their lives. It is, however, completely unclear in psychological research what makes a hug memorable compared to other hugs.

A study published in the scientific journal PLoS ONE investigated which factors shape a hug's memory (Dueren and co-workers, 2026). In the study, “Why we hug: Individual differences predict emotional touch memories,” the research team, led by scientist Anna Lena Dueren from the University of Bristol in the UK, analyzed data from a large-scale hugging survey with more than 15,000 participants. For the study, the scientists recruited male and female volunteers through BBC public broadcasting programs and other media.

The volunteers, ages 18 to 92, answered an online questionnaire about hugging and touch in general, as well as about several personality and other psychological factors. The volunteers were asked whether they remembered a specific hug for its positive effects on them. If they answered “Yes” to this question, they had to pick a phrase from a list of phrases to describe why they remembered that hug. The possible phrases were:

In addition, volunteers answered questionnaires about attachment anxiety and avoidance, body acceptance and body perception, whether their childhood bedtime routine included a hug from their parents, whether they had difficulties hugging, whether they disliked hugging, empathy, hugging frequency, and whether volunteers used hugging as a greeting.

Overall, about two-thirds of volunteers—10,457 people—reported they remembered a specific hug for its positive emotional effect.

The three most common reasons to remember a hug for female volunteers were:

Very similarly, the three most common reasons to remember a hug for male volunteers were:

In addition, the scientists used advanced statistical models to find out how individual differences and experiences shape how people remember hugs. The analyses showed that people who disliked hugs, had difficulty hugging, or avoided attachment were less likely to remember a hug for its positive emotional impact. Volunteers who frequently hugged as a greeting and those who were very empathetic were more likely to remember a hug for its positive emotional impact; so were people with high attachment anxiety and high scores in the body perception questionnaire. The other factors showed no effects.

Taken together, the research shows that nearly seven in 10 people recall a specific hug because of how it made them feel. However, whether someone remembers a special hug depends on several individual factors, such as the empathy level and attachment style. These findings highlight how emotionally significant hugs can be, as we may carry the memory of some special hugs for the rest of our lives!

Dueren, A. L., Jenkinson, P. M., Vafeiadou, A., Koukoutsakis, A., Hammond, C., Bowling, N. C., Fotopoulou, A., & Banissy, M. J. (2026). Why we hug: Individual differences predict emotional touch memories. PloS one, 21(10), e0359868. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0359868

Ocklenburg, S. (2024). The Psychology and Neuroscience of Hugging - A Multidisciplinary Perspective. Springer: Berlin.

#4788. Here Are the 7 Best Long-Sleeve Shirts for Cold-Weather Workouts

Stay dry, cool, and protected during your workouts with our favorite long-sleeve shirts.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

FALL IS HERE, and with it, the chill is starting to hit the air. This change in temperature shifts the spotlight to what we think is the unsung hero of your fall and winter workout wardrobe, especially when it comes to your workouts: the long-sleeve T-shirt.

Whether you’re trying to ward off goosebumps or protect your skin from the sun, long-sleeve shirts are a solid choice for training. Many are made from the same performance fabrics as our favorite workout shirts; they can wick moisture and keep you cooler than a wool layer while offering more coverage than a short-sleeve tee.

Collectively, the Men’s Health editorial team has trained in dozens of long-sleeve shirts and pooled our experience to bring you seven picks for different types of training.

The long-sleeve sibling of our best overall workout shirt also snags the top spot in our roundup of long-sleeve workout shirts. After all, it’s virtually the same shirt, just better suited for fall and winter workouts.

The Strato Tech Tee is among the softest shirts I’ve ever worn, and after a year of consistent use, mine still looks, feels, and performs much like it did during my first week of testing. Its four-way-stretch fabric contributes to its excellent comfort, and despite the shirt’s paper-thin feel, it was surprisingly effective at wicking moisture during our sweatiest workouts.

Because it’s lightweight, keeps sweat at bay, and is versatile enough to double as an everyday shirt, the Strato Tech earns its near-$70 price tag. It’s the kind of staple worth investing in.

The skin-tight fit of compression gear doesn’t appeal to everyone, but compression shirts offer plenty of utility. You can wear one on its own, under a short-sleeve tee for a fall or winter workout, or as a base layer for skiing and hiking.

Dick’s Sporting Goods’ DSG compression crew is a good option for skeptical buyers. It costs $30 per shirt and comes in more than 15 color options. The trade-off for that affordability is slightly less comfort. In particular, the seams that run along the arms can be a little annoying. It also runs a bit longer than I prefer, so I opted to tuck mine in.

Read More: Best Compression Shirts, Tested by Us

Gymshark has cemented itself as a major player in the fitness apparel space, not just because of the quality of its clothing, but also because its marketing and product lines often reflect what the current generation of gymgoers are wearing.

The Power Long Sleeve T-Shirt is a good example. It leans into the current pump-cover trend, where lifters wear oversized layers at the start of a workout and shed them once they’re warmed up and pumped. The Power Tee fits oversized but true to size and keeps the look simple, save for “Gymshark” printed across the back. It also comes in four colors.

Because it’s made from 95% cotton, expect it to hold onto more heat and sweat than a technical training shirt. I wouldn’t reach for it for hard runs or conditioning sessions, but for lifting, it works well either as a standalone shirt or as an extra layer to keep you warm between sets.

When people think of Under Armour, they often think of compression gear, so its HeatGear line—a collection designed to provide coverage while keeping athletes cool—is a natural pick for anyone who wants to keep their arms covered during spring and summer workouts.

Athletes who wear pads, trail runners looking for protection from brush, and even people with sun-sensitive skin can all benefit from the extra coverage. HeatGear fabric is ventilated and described by Under Armour as “ultra-light,” so the shirt offers protection without adding much bulk or warmth. And at $40 with 16 color options, it’s an affordable, versatile choice that works as either a standalone training shirt or a base layer.

Co-owned by Mark Wahlberg, Municipal is a lifestyle and fitness brand that makes gear for activities including training, golf, and running. The Enduro Stretch LS can work as a running shirt, but its minimal branding and simple design make it versatile enough for lifting, errands, or casual wear, too.

It has the hallmarks of a solid workout shirt: super stretch, moisture-wicking fabric, and a lightweight feel, all from a 100% polyester construction. The ribbed cuffs bring a lot more durability to the sleeves and a little style, so that you get more use out of this piece.

Municipal is still a relatively young brand, and the Enduro Stretch LS is only available in three colors, with fewer customer reviews than some of the more established options on this list. At this price, that makes it a slightly less proven pick, but its simple design and performance-focused construction give it plenty of appeal for runners and lifters alike.

If most of your training takes place outside, this is the shirt worth investing in. Ten Thousand—a brand that’s made it onto our best workout shirt and best workout shorts lists—built the Tactical Long Sleeve with sun protection, odor-blocking technology, and micro-mesh fabric designed to help regulate body temperature.

The shirt also uses flatlock seams, which lie flatter against the skin and help reduce irritation while reinforcing high-stress areas. The upper back, or yoke, is reinforced to better withstand ruck sacks, plate carriers, and weighted vests. There are a few trade-offs: It only comes in two colors (black and green), the care instructions are a little finicky, and it costs close to $100.

The Tactical is one of those buy-once, cry-once purchases that cost more up front but may save you money if it holds up longer than cheaper shirts. And Ten Thousand does have a one-year guarantee on their clothes. That said, not everyone wants to—or can— spend that much on a workout shirt, and you certainly don’t need one this rugged for every outdoor training session.

If you like wearing sleeves year-round, it’s worth investing in a lightweight shirt that keeps you covered without trapping too much heat. Barbell Apparel’s Arid Drop Hem Long Sleeve is made from a blend of bamboo, polyester, and a touch of spandex for added stretch and mobility. Customers describe it as lightweight and flattering, which tracks for a brand that built its name making clothes for people with more athletic builds.

Designed for warm-weather use, the Arid also includes odor control and UV protection, while its looser fit through the torso helps keep the fabric from clinging as you sweat. Aesthetically, it fits in just about anywhere, and its two neutral color options—black and a grayish blue—make it easier to get more mileage out of the hefty price tag.

Most workout shirts are made primarily from synthetic materials such as polyester, nylon, and elastane. These fabrics tend to dry faster than cotton and can be engineered to move moisture away from your skin, which helps keep the shirt from feeling soaked during a workout.

Cotton, by comparison, absorbs and holds onto more moisture, which can leave a shirt feeling heavy and damp and may contribute to chafing or irritation. That doesn’t mean cotton has no place in workout gear. Some shirts blend in a small amount to soften the fabric and improve comfort. An all-cotton shirt may be less appealing for sweaty sessions, but a little cotton in the blend isn’t necessarily a drawback.

Odor control generally comes down to two things: how quickly the fabric dries and whether it has been treated to limit odor-causing bacteria. Moisture-wicking, quick-drying fabrics can help keep sweat from sitting against your skin for as long, but the fabric itself doesn’t automatically prevent odor.

Some manufacturers also treat fibers with antimicrobial technologies designed to slow bacterial growth. Silver, copper, and zinc-based treatments are common examples. Other brands use different chemical or bio-based treatments to achieve a similar effect. If odor control matters to you, look for a specific antimicrobial or anti-odor claim rather than assuming every synthetic shirt has it.

You probably don’t need to obsess over seams, but they’re worth paying attention to if you’re prone to chafing. Look for flatlock seams, which sit flatter and feel less bulky against the skin, as well as thoughtful seam placement in high-friction areas.

The armpit is one of the more annoying places to have bulky stitching, which is why some workout shirts use raglan sleeves. Instead of a traditional sleeve seam that starts at the shoulder, raglan sleeves extend up toward the collar and create diagonal seams across the upper chest and back. That construction can reduce irritation and allow for more freedom of movement.

No. Many long-sleeve workout shirts are lightweight enough to wear comfortably during spring and summer, depending on the temperature and your personal preference.

There are also practical reasons to cover up in warm weather. Long sleeves can help shield your arms from direct sun and offer some protection from rough brush, branches, gravel, and other elements if you train outdoors or spend a lot of time on the trails.

As a fitness writer, personal trainer, and guy who likes to train, I spend a lot of time in workout clothes, usually while lifting or running. I’m fortunate that companies send me samples throughout the year—always with no strings attached—to test, and Men’s Health will occasionally ship specific products to my house for dedicated testing.

Creating this list was a collective effort between the Men’s Health editorial team and me, including Fitness and Reviews Editor Charles Thorp, NASM, Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan. Our standard testing protocol is to wear each shirt for at least two weeks and put it through common exercises like pull-ups, push-ups, and deadlifts. At the time I wrote this article, I was also logging 15 to 25 miles of running per week across the treadmill, road, and local trails, so I rotated several of these shirts through those sessions to see how they held up.

We take notes on each shirt’s style, fit, comfort, price, versatility, and performance, including stretch, moisture management, and breathability. We also pay attention to sizing—whether a shirt fits true to size or runs large or small—and how the fabric holds up after repeated workouts and washes. What we don’t do is chase trends. Our goal is to recommend shirts that perform well now and should still make sense years from now.

Andrew Gutman, NASM-CPT is a journalist with a decade of experience covering fitness and nutrition. His work has been published in Men's Health, Men's Journal, Muscle & Fitness, and Gear Patrol. Outside of writing, Andrew trains in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, helps coach his gym's kickboxing team, and enjoys reading and cooking.

Charles Thorp is the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he shares the best product recommendations in gym equipment, recovery tools, supplements, and more. Following an early life in athletics, Charles became a NASM-certified trainer and began writing programs alongside the most respected coaches in the world.   Since entering the world of fitness content, Charles has had the opportunity to learn from and train alongside high performance individuals from the NFL, UFC, NBA, Formula 1, CrossFit, US Olympics, and Navy SEALs. When he’s not writing about training programs or gear, he can be seen at the gym or in the wild, putting them to the test.

#4787. Kia’s PV5 electric campervan has two beds and a fully equipped kitchen [Images]

Kia’s electric campervan, based on the PV5, includes two double beds, a 200 W solar panel, and a fully equipped kitchen.

The PV5, Kia’s first 100% electric van, has been a huge success for the Korean automaker. After launching it at the end of last year, the PV5 has already become Europe’s top-selling small (C-segment) electric van.

Based on its modular skateboard platform, called E-GMP.S, Kia can easily swap body styles to build custom configurations.

Although the PV5 is primarily sold in Passenger for everyday driving and Cargo for business use, Kia said the platform unlocks “endless possibilities” for different body styles and conversions, including a full-on electric campervan.

Wellhouse Leisure, a family-run campervan manufacturer based in the UK, revealed the Kia PV5 i-Camper.

The fully electric campervan is “now built and ready to view,” the company said. Based on the PV5 Cargo Plus, the campervan measures 4.69 m long, 1.89 m wide, and 1.99 m tall, which is about the size of a Ford Custom.

Although that’s pretty small for a camper, it offers more than you’d expect. Inside, the PV5 i-Camper includes two double beds with an elevating roof, a full kitchen setup, and a 200 W solar panel.

The sliding seat system enables the two rear seats to fold flat to form a bed and can be removed entirely. The upper bed, under the pop-up roof, has “more comfy” Froli Springs.

In the kitchen, you’ll find a sink with a tap and an electric water pump, two induction burners, a 42 L refrigerator, cabinets and storage spaces, and an optional microwave.

This EV would be a huge hit if imported into the US. Maybe after the huge order backlog has subsided Kia will consider importing the van to the States.

The vehicle also has a lithium leisure battery and a 12V supply, so you don’t need to use the vehicle’s main battery while camping.

It also comes with vehicle-to-load, letting you power external electrical devices, an e-bike, or even a campsite.

The PV5 Plus Long Range model uses a 71.2 kWh battery, providing a WLTP range of up to 247 miles. However, the added equipment will impact the range in the campervan conversion. Charging the battery from 10% to 80% takes around 30 minutes using a DC fast charger.

In the UK, Wellhouse Leisure lists the PV5 electric campervan starting at £63,000, or about $84,000.

#4786. Why Living with Endometriosis May Double Your Odds of Migraine

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In a new analysis, researchers found females with endometriosis were 2.3 times more likely to also have migraine, and they said the two conditions may share a pain pathway involving nerves and inflammation.Recognizing that connection earlier could lead to coordinated care for both conditions, the researchers said.The analysis, presented at the American Neurological Association (ANA) Annual Meeting in San Diego on October 20, included more than 13 million females. The research hasn’t yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to what lines the uterus grows outside the uterus, Mallory Stuparich, MD, a gynecologic surgeon at MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, California, told Healthline. Stuparich was not involved in the study.Yohannes Woubishet Woldeamanuel, MD, lead author of the study and assistant professor of neurology at Mayo Clinic Arizona, told Healthline that migraine also involves more than one part of the body.“Migraine is more than a headache,” he said.Headache is one symptom, Woldeamanuel said, but migraine can also cause sensory, motor, and balance symptoms.“Migraine is a little complex. It’s a multiple-nervous system involving a condition,” he said.

Stuparich said endometriosis pain typically develops in 2 ways. The first starts in the lesions themselves.“There are inflammatory markers that are created by the endometriosis lesions themselves, and those inflammatory markers can irritate the nerves that live close by the lesions,” she said.The second involves the nervous system, Stuparich said. Scar tissue can grow its own nerve supply, and years of chronic pain can change how the nervous system responds. That adaptation can “perpetuate pain or make people feel sensations that normally wouldn’t be painful,” she said.Stuparich said the inflammatory and immune processes involved in endometriosis have “pretty significant overlap in the setting of migraines.”

One possible link between the two conditions is calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a chemical messenger that helps transmit pain signals, the researchers said.CGRP plays a key role in migraine attacks, Woldeamanuel said, and blocking it reduces those attacks. CGRP medications work by blocking the sites where CGRP attaches or by binding to CGRP itself.Researchers have also found CGRP in endometriosis tissue.

A 2024 study published in Science Translational Medicine found CGRP in endometriosis lesions from both people and mice. In mice, blocking CGRP signaling reduced pain and reduced lesion size.

Other studies point to shared biology between the two conditions:

Stuparich said she was “not surprised at all” by the finding because it matches what she sees in her own patients.“We see this overlap of patients who have endometriosis also having migraines,” she said.Stuparich said the science still has gaps. She noted that nothing has been proven conclusively in peer-reviewed research yet, but the way both diseases behave supports a connection.“It makes sense that there would be overlap,” she said.

Endometriosis and migraine are treated by different specialists, so the overlap is easy to miss, Woldeamanuel said.For the analysis, researchers at Mayo Clinic Arizona reviewed 35 studies published over 50 years, comparing migraine rates among 207,675 females with endometriosis and 12,963,120 females without the condition.Short-term health records miss up to 90% of that overlap, according to the analysis. Migraine rates in females with endometriosis changed depending on how each study identified migraine.“This data is hiding,” Woldeamanuel said.

“These two clinics are siloed. One clinic doesn’t ask about the other condition. They just focus on their own specialty,” Woldeamanuel said.The findings of the analysis have not been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

Some treatments already overlap, Stuparich said. Hormonal birth control “can sometimes be used to treat menstrually associated migraines,” she said.Stuparich said she has heard anecdotally of patients whose endometriosis symptoms improved after they started CGRP medications for migraine, though long-term data are still lacking.The researchers said the findings support studying whether existing CGRP-blocking migraine medications could also relieve endometriosis pain, potentially offering one treatment for both conditions.Woldeamanuel leads a planned Mayo Clinic trial testing one of those medications, rimegepant (Nurtec ODT), for endometriosis pain. The trial will also track migraine days in participants who have both conditions. It’s expected to finish in 2031, according to ClinicalTrials.gov.

People who suspect they have both conditions can take steps now to get them treated together, Stuparich said.Patients can raise the connection themselves, Stuparich said. She suggested a starting point for each appointment:

Patients can also ask for an early referral to the other specialist so both conditions get coordinated care, Woldeamanuel said. “The earlier it’s diagnosed, the better it’s managed,” he said.Stuparich said doctors are moving away from viewing endometriosis as only a gynecologic disorder because it can affect the whole body.“It is a whole body systemic neuroinflammatory neuroimmune disorder,” she said.

#4784. Puffer Jackets, Wetsuits, Headphones, and More: The Coolest Gear Our Editors Are Testing This Month

Gear that can actually handle colder weather.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Welcome to the MH Gear Report, where Men’s Health gear and tech experts find the coolest new releases in gear, technology, home goods, and more. Plus, some insights into new gear we’ve been testing lately.

THE HOLIDAYS ARE fast approaching, and we’re already prepping for Black Friday and Cyber Monday here at Men’s Health. But that doesn’t mean our gear testing stops. In fact, we’re in a switch right now with the cooler weather and getting to finally test things like puffer jackets, midlayers, and wetsuits.

While we’re always testing products like headphones or running shoes no matter where the calendar is at, these seasonal shifts give us the chance to dig into some other activities and regimens. And then getting to translate all those experiences to you so you know what’s good, what’s not, and what’s just ok.

Nothing finally built a pro-level pair of cans and there’s a lot to love: physical buttons, great battery life (30+ hours), improved active-noise cancelling that’s really good, and the signature transparent look that the brand has become known for. They are a bit heavy (you expect that from pro headphones) and the ear cushioning is slightly less firm than we’d like, but these have been a pair we’re going to keep wearing most days.

The Adios Pro 5 is lighter and more responsive than the Pro 4, and has a reworked upper (that helps create a more locked-in fit) and a new midsole foam formulation that feels closer to firm than cushy. Lots of runners gunning for a race PR will love the Pro 5 for their goal event and their fastest training days.

Read More: Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 Review

“I love this lightweight insulated jacket,” Creative Director Jamie Prokell says. “It’s the perfect transitional coat—somewhere between a down puffer and a bomber, the Lapwing looks stylish on its own and provides the right amount of warmth without the bulk.”

Later in the season, its low-profile design also makes it a great liner under a shell. And you can feel good knowing that its REPREVE insulation and recycled performance fabrics work well while also being better for the planet.

Ciele makes more than just running hats, and this pair of run shorts is already a great offering with the 2-in-1 compression-like short underneath and a very light and flowy short on top. But given a more reflective detailing treatment for the Nite Rite capsule, these bad boys are perfect for the shorter days we’re now getting.

The U-zip wetsuit is a fairly new offering from a few brands, and Patagonia’s version is one we’ve just started testing given the season. Like all Patagonia wetsuits, it’s made neoprene-free (which is petroleum-based) with Yulex natural rubber and synthetic rubber. So this easier-to-get-into suit is also a bit better for the planet.

Utilizing Polartec’s Alpha Direct fleece (which was originally developed for U.S. Special Forces), this active quarter zip is built for movement. The weight-to-warmth ratio is serious, and the beauty of the open-mesh fleece fabric is that it’s great at insulating but also at dumping heat when things get too warm. While lots of brands are using this material right now, this is one of the more unique offerings we’ve tried in the QZ (most are hoodies with scuba-style hoods).

While the screenless fitness tracker trend certainly took hold in 2026, there’s still lots of folks who want some screen. The new Fitbit Edge is the successor to the Charge 6 and leans into the design that Fitbit became known for.

Out of nowhere last month, Yeti dropped a performance apparel line made up of four pieces: a down jacket, a rain jacket, a zip-up fleece, and a quarter-zip fleece. It’s a pivot into outdoor apparel we can’t say we expected, but it does make a bit of sense. We’ve just gotten pieces in for testing and plan to have a full review up soon, but these do look and feel the part. Yet they do come with the premium Yeti price tag as well.

Yes, Skechers has made a carbon-plated race shoe and it’s pretty solid. Lightweight at 5.9 oz, the woven jacquard upper is comfy and the closure system allows for a secure fit—it’s also got that slightly off-center lacing to help avoid hot spots on the top of the foot, which I find meaningful. I think it might be my pick for a 5K turkey trot later this month.

#4783. Volkswagen’s EV battery recall reaches over 85,000, with Audi now included

Volkswagen’s latest recall now extends to Audi, affecting nearly 13,000 Q4 E-Tron and Q4 Sportback E-Tron vehicles globally. And just like with the ID.4, owners are being told to limit charging to 80% of the battery’s capacity.

Earlier this month, Volkswagen issued a recall with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) impacting 22,524 ID.4 electric SUVs, model years 2023 to 2026.

Official information from the German Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA) revealed shortly after that several thousand more VW Group electric vehicles are affected worldwide.

In three separate recalls now under investigation by the KBA, 72,668 VW Group EVs were included worldwide, including 9,881 in Germany.

The recall affects certain batches of the ID. Buzz, ID.3, ID.4, and ID.7 models produced between 2022 and 2025, as well as Cupra Born models from 2022 to 2024.

On October 27, VW Group added another electric vehicle to the KBA recall database. The latest recall impacts 12,734 Audi Q4 E-Tron and Q4 Sportback E-Tron vehicles globally, including just one in Germany. In total, Volkswagen’s battery recall now affects 85,402 EVs globally.

In the letter sent to the NHTSA on October 23, Volkswagen Group of America said it was issuing a recall affecting 9,048 Audi Q4 E-Tron and Q4 Sportback E-Tron vehicles in the US model years 2024 to 2025.

The recall stems from the risk of the battery overheating and potentially causing a fire under certain conditions when charged to over 80% of its limit.

Volkswagen said in a safety recall report with the NHTSA that “certain charging profiles combined with a state of charge over 80% may trigger thermal propagation.”

While the root cause is unknown, Volkswagen urged owners to limit charging to 80%. Owners of affected vehicles received an email saying VW “intends to apply a temporary vehicle setting that limits charging to 80%,” unless they opted out by October 21.

The safety recall follows Audi’s Product Safety Committee being informed of battery thermal events involving other Volkswagen Group EVs that use the same batteries as the Audi Q4 E-Tron.

Following an internal investigation, Audi found the same battery and production characteristics as the impacted VW Group vehicles. Audi said the majority of these were produced for the North American market.

Audi is not aware of any claims, crashes, fires, injuries, or deaths associated with the Q4 E-Tron’s battery issue.

Dang it. I posted this concern in the other article that covered the ID.4 that Audi Q4 would be next. And here we are. I guess I'm going to have to call the hotline and see if mine is part of the recall. This is starting out just like the Chevy Bolt fiasco. I had a 2020 Bolt that eventually got a new battery pack but it was a battle with GM till they finally got it done. My guess is the VW group will do the same thing here. And oh by the way selling the car while this recall is in question will be a no go. Ugghh.

The root cause has yet to be determined, and until a remedy is available, Audi is advising owners to limit charging to 80%.

Owners in the US can take their vehicles to an authorized Audi dealer, where the dealer will run a diagnostic check on the battery. If needed, the dealer will impose a temporary state-of-charge limit to 80%.

Audi expects to mail out interim letters notifying owners of the safety risks on December 18, 2026. Additional letters will send additional letters once a remedy is available.

Owners can contact Audi’s customer service at 1-800-253-2834 with questions or concerns. Audi’s recall number is 93SK. You can also contact the NHTSA Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit nhtsa.gov for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V698.

#4782. Ambience Is the Silent Influencer

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 7, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

“No object is so ugly that, under certain conditions of light and shade, or proximity to other things, it will not look beautiful.” —Oscar Wilde

Ambience is defined as an atmosphere, or a surrounding influence. It involves subjective experience of the outside world through sense perception. The atmosphere or ambience of a certain situation contributes to the aesthetic experience.

We appreciate the way in which various elements come together to influence the aesthetic experience. For example, our appreciation of food is inseparable from the whole ambience orchestrated by a few other ingredients: table setting and decoration, the environment in which we are eating, music, the occasion, time of the day, and so on.

Our ordinary experience is seldom obtained through a single sensory source. What we appreciate is not any single sensation (a smell and texture) but the way in which various elements come together to provide ambience. That is, taste is inseparable from smell and texture. The rich aroma of Starbucks coffee would likely clash with the delicate, fresh scent of sushi, resulting in a mismatched sensory experience. The taste of a very expensive wine wouldn’t be the same if we drank it out of a paper cup.

In the context of restaurants, consumer perceptions are shaped by a confluence of sensory inputs (sight, sound, touch, taste, and smell), each contributing to the overall perception of value and quality. Taste is rarely experienced in isolation. Visual presentation, aroma, and texture all play pivotal roles in shaping flavor perception (Spence, 2016).

Aesthetic experiences are also socially framed, such as viewing a painting or theatrical work in an appropriate setting (museum or theater). Artworks in museums are rated as more pleasant and evoke longer viewing times, whereas those viewed on computer screens are rated as less interesting, memorable, and arousing (Pelowski, 2017). Art collectors know that museum exhibitions can add prestige to an artist or an artwork’s value.

An amusing illustration of this occurred when, in 2007, acclaimed violinist Joshua Bell agreed to participate in an experiment conducted by The Washington Post. In the experiment, Bell, wearing jeans and a baseball cap, nonchalantly played his $3.5 million Stradivarius violin during rush hour in the subway. Most passersby barely noticed him and gave no indication of realizing that they were in the presence of an accomplished artist. However, when people see Joshua Bell dressed up in a concert hall, they highly appreciate his talent, even though he is playing the same instrument and the same music. This discrepancy arises because our brain evaluates the same sounds differently in different situations.

The importance of ambience in mood regulation encourages one to be more attentive to their surrounding atmospheres. For example, coffee shops often play laid-back folk music or chill-out electronic music to calm their patrons without interfering with their conversations or other quiet activities. In the context of a dining experience, soft, warm lighting often evokes intimacy and comfort, fostering a sense of luxury and exclusivity.

Research in consumer behavior has shown that creating certain atmospheres in cafés, restaurants, or shops can influence sales (North, 1999). For instance, music plays a pivotal role. The pace of background music can influence how customers eat and drink in a restaurant. When a song plays at a fast pace, we move faster. When slower music is played, customers spend more time browsing. Slower tempos encourage diners to linger, enjoy, and spend more. Classical compositions often convey sophistication and have been shown to encourage patrons to linger longer and spend more.

North, A.C., Hargreaves, D.J., McKendrick, J. (1999). The influence of in-store music on wine selections. J. Appl. Psychol., 84 (2), pp. 271-276.

Pelowski, M., Forster, M., Tinio, P. P. L., Scholl, M., & Leder, H. (2017). Beyond the lab: An examination of key factors influencing interaction with ‘real’ and museum-based Art. Psychol. Aesthet. Creat Arts. 11, 245–264.

Spence, C., Okajima, K., Cheok, A.D., Petit, O., Michel, C. (2016). Eating with our eyes: From visual hunger to digital satiation. Brain Cogn. 110:53-63.

#4781. Can L-Theanine Supplements Actually Help You Relax and Focus?

The science isn’t as clear as supplement ads suggest.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

A SUPPLEMENT THAT helps you relax and focus sounds like a no-brainer. Some supplement companies are suggesting that L-theanine is your answer. True, dietitians don’t exactly hate this supplement. There are some reasons to suggest L-theanine could do all the above to a certain degree. But there’s a significantly cheaper alternative everyone keeps overlooking. More on that below.

L-THEANINE IS A compound found in tea that allegedly helps you relax and focus.

“Have a demanding task at work late in the day but don't want coffee jitters? Tea's combination of caffeine and L-theanine can give you a calm yet alert mental state that could help boost productivity and effectiveness,” says Kate Ingram, MPH, RD, citing a popular study on caffeine and L-theanine published in Cureus. In supplement form, L-theanine typically has about 200 mg per serving. For context, that’s quite a bit more than the standard 6 milligrams or so in a cup of tea.

L-THEANINE HAS A rare ability to pass through the blood-brain barrier. This semipermeable barricade protects your brain from toxins and other dangerous substances. Not all medications and supplements can safely pass through and affect the brain.

Since L-theanine can pass through to the brain, companies have marketed the compound as a supplement for peak cognitive performance. There’s some science to suggest brain benefits.

In clinical trials, 100 to 400 milligrams of L-theanine produced a “small but statistically significant” improvement in tasks involving visual attention. When paired with caffeine, people also showed greater cognitive performance than without. The cognitive benefits of L-theanine may even show up after a single dose. People who took one 200-milligram dose 30 to 60 minutes before a cognitive test showed higher scores in attention.

Like a good cup of tea, an L-theanine supplement may reduce anxiety and stress. One review suggested 200 to 400 milligrams of L-theanine could calm people who regularly encounter stressful situations.

Researchers decades ago also suggested that people who supplement with L-theanine may sleep more soundly and potentially stave off mental decline. “But the key word is suggest,” says dietitian Perri Halperin, RD. In recent years, scientists reviewing claims of L-theanine increasing alpha waves in the brain to improve sleep quality have found that “findings are often inconsistent.”

One review suggested that L-theanine supplementation could help immune system function—in livestock. There are also studies finding evidence that L-theanine helped to reduce the risk of cancer. Again, in animals only. No supplement has yet been proven to boost immunity in people.

“L-THEANINE IS GENERALLY recognized as safe; however, it is always best to consult your healthcare provider before starting any supplement,” says Ingram. This is especially the case if you have underlying health conditions or are taking other medications. L-theanine supplements could interact with some anti-anxiety, blood-pressure, and sleep meds. Side effects include headaches, dizziness, nausea, and jitteriness.

AS INGRAM PUTS it, “why start a supplement when you can just have a cup of tea?” Plus, with tea you have so many other health benefits such as its potential to improve gut health, promote weight loss, and protect you against chronic disease, Ingram says.

Bottom line: You might get a more set dose of L-theanine if you take it in supplement form, but you'll be paying a lot for something you can get from just brewing a cup of tea. "Tea is certainly a cost-effective way to give it a try,” Ingram says. And, as always, talk to your doctor or a registered dietitian before beginning any type of supplement to ensure that it's something that will work best for you.

#4780. Dems introduce new $15,000 EV tax credit bill that has no chance — and that’s a problem

Rep. Greg Landsman (D-OH) wants to bring back the federal EV tax credit and double it. His new bill, the “21st Century Vehicle Choice Act” (H.R. 10881), would offer up to $15,000 on a new electric vehicle and $8,000 on a used one, and it would make both credits permanent.

The problem is that the bill has virtually no chance of becoming law anytime soon. And if EV shoppers start holding out for it, it could end up hurting the market it’s trying to help.

Landsman introduced H.R. 10881 on October 22. It was referred to three House committees (Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Natural Resources), and as of today, it doesn’t have a single cosponsor.

The big change is to the new clean vehicle credit, Section 30D of the tax code. Under the Inflation Reduction Act, the $7,500 credit came in two $3,750 halves: one for meeting critical mineral sourcing requirements and one for battery components. Landsman’s bill doubles each half to $7,500, for a maximum of $15,000.

It also deletes the termination dates. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act killed the new and used EV credits for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and the home charger credit after June 30, 2026. Striking those dates would revive all three credits with no expiration.

The bill doesn’t touch the rest of 30D. North American final assembly, the $55,000 MSRP cap on cars and $80,000 cap on SUVs, pickups, and vans, and the foreign entity of concern rules all stay. So the full $15,000 would only go to EVs that clear both sourcing tests, which has always been a short list.

The rest of the bill is reports. Commerce would deliver a “Vehicle Choice Report” on vehicle variety and ownership costs, and the Department of Energy would file five years of critical minerals reports.

The most interesting part is a DOE study of “gasoline super-users,” defined as the top 10% of light-duty vehicle owners by gas consumption. The study would map the regions where they’re concentrated and their 100 most-used routes, then track charger availability along those routes every year for five years. Coltura, which backs the bill, says the highest-mileage drivers spend over 10% of household income on fuel.

Republicans control both the House and the Senate, and they’re the ones who just repealed these credits. President Trump signed that repeal.

Even if Democrats flip the House and Senate in next week’s midterms, a bill restoring EV credits would still need to get through a veto. So realistically, nothing like this happens before 2029.

It’s also a rerun. Landsman introduced the exact same “21st Century Vehicle Choice Act” as H.R. 10046 on October 25, 2024, 11 days before that year’s election. It got zero cosponsors and died in committee. This version landed 12 days before the November 3 midterms.

This is where the bill can do real damage. EV buyers are extremely sensitive to tax credit timing, and the last year proved it.

When the credit was about to disappear, buyers rushed in, and Q3 2025 became the best quarter ever for US EV sales, with market share topping 10% for the first time. Then the floor dropped out. Hyundai’s Ioniq 5 sales fell 63% the month after the credit ended.

The market is only now crawling back. According to Cox Automotive, US EV sales hit 262,649 units in Q3 2026, up 6.1% from Q2 but still down 39.5% year-over-year, at a 6.4% share of new vehicle sales. Tesla’s Model Y and Model 3 still dominate, but Toyota, Rivian, and Hyundai are growing again.

That recovery is fragile. A headline promising “$15,000 off your next EV” is exactly what makes a shopper on the fence decide to wait a year or two.

And waiting gets you nothing. The new credits would only apply to vehicles placed in service after the bill is enacted, so there’s no retroactive payout for buying now. If you already claimed the credit once, you’d get $0 anyway.

Meanwhile, the deals on the lot are real. Automakers have been cutting prices to make up for the lost credit, like Hyundai, which cut the 2026 Ioniq 5 by nearly $10,000 on some trims.

At Electrek, our position has always been clear: we think EVs are a net positive and ICE vehicles have unpriced externalities. Therefore, we will take whatever we can get to encourage EV sales, but our preferred approach would be a carbon tax on ICE vehicles.

We’ve been clear that policy shapes this market. Killing the $7,500 credit is the main reason US EV sales collapsed. Consumers didn’t suddenly decide they hate EVs. So we’re all for bringing incentives back.

But this bill is messaging. It has zero cosponsors and no CBO score, and it dropped two weeks before an election, just like the identical version two years ago.

They should focus on rooftop and community solar tax credits and initiatives. With rising electric rates, helping people alleviate those would be vastly more popular than EV subsidies.

To be fair, some of it is smart. The lower income caps and the once-per-taxpayer limit go after the most common criticism of the old credit, that it subsidized wealthy households buying their second or third EV. And the “super-user” study is the best idea in the bill. Getting a high-mileage driver out of a gas pickup does far more for fuel costs and emissions than putting a low-mileage commuter in their second Tesla. If Democrats want to rebuild EV policy in 2029, that’s where they should start.

The problem is that people will hear the headline number. If you need a car now and an EV fits your life, buy it now and take the deals that are on the table. Don’t plan your purchase around a bill that has no path to passing for at least two years.

Will Democrats come back with a real, cosponsored EV plan before 2028? I don’t know, but I suspect that the US will continue to fall behind the rest of the world when it comes to EV adoption.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, with or without a tax credit. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4778. Used EVs are suddenly hot sellers — Here are the top SUVs for under $25,000

Don’t want to pay full price? Used EVs with low miles, like the Hyundai IONIQ 5 and Ford Mustang Mach-E, are selling on the secondhand market for $25,000 or less.

With a flood of electric cars returning from lease this year and soaring gas prices, used EVs are suddenly flying off the lot.

Used EV sales rose to a record 3.3% of total used vehicle sales last month, up from 2.9% in August, according to Cox Automotive.

Used ICE vehicle sales, on the other hand, dropped 4.4% in September as buyers flocked to more efficient options.

As expected, Tesla remains the leading used EV brand, followed by Ford, Chevrolet, Hyundai, and BMW.

By model, the Nissan Ariya led growth, with sales up 42.5% in September, followed by the Chevy Equinox EV (+41.9%), Kia EV9 (+36.2%), and Chevy Blazer EV (+30.2%), while the Ford Mustang Mach-E (+14.7%) and Tesla Model Y (+13.8 %) also saw more demand.

With more options to choose from, which one is best for you? To help you decide, Edmunds, which has tested nearly all of them, put together a list of four top used electric SUVs available for under $25,000.

The first one on the list was the Chevy Equinox EV, or as GM used to call it, “America’s most affordable 315+ range” electric vehicle.

After it arrived in 2024, the Chevy Equinox EV quickly became one of the top-selling electric vehicles in the US outside Tesla, winning over buyers with enough space for a family and plenty of driving range at an affordable price.

The Chevy Equinox EV offers up to 319 miles of EPA-estimated driving range. It’s a great fit for those looking for a smaller, more efficient SUV that still offers plenty of interior space.

Edmunds says it’s worth upgrading to the 2LT trim, which adds heated front seats and a heated steering wheel, a wireless phone charger, adaptive cruise control, and a 360-degree HD Surround Vision camera system.

Next on the list was the Ford Mustang Mach-E, which has also remained a top seller since it went on sale in 2021.

Ford tapped into its iconic Mustang nameplate to help attract new buyers. The Mustang Mach-E came well equipped with a large 15.5″ infotainment screen with Wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto and Ford Co-Pilot360 Assist+.

While the GT is the most fun to drive, Edmunds said the Premium trim may be your best bet. It still offers plenty of performance while adding standard features like heated front seats and a heated steering wheel.

It’s also worth upgrading to the extended-range battery pack, which offers up to 320 miles of range on the Premium RWD model. You should be able to find used 2021 to 2023 Mach-E’s for under $25,000.

Another top-selling electric SUV, the Hyundai IONIQ 5 continues to win over buyers with its bold design, long-range capabilities, fast charging, and a surprisingly spacious interior.

Edmunds says plenty of used 2022 to 2024 IONIQ 5s with low mileage are available for under $25,000.

While the base SE Standard Range is the cheapest, it only offers an EPA range of 220 miles. Upgrading to the Extended Range battery, which is used on all other trims, provides up to 303 miles of range.

The Volkswagen ID.4 went on sale in the US in 2021 as one of the earlier mainstream electric SUVs.

It also just happens that many EVs are coming off lease so the inventory is plentiful combined with high gas price. Perfect storm.

#4777. The Complete Guide to the Best Dumbbells for Your Home Gym

For a complete home gym setup, you need a proper set of dumbbells—period.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

IF YOU WANT a complete home gym setup, you need a proper set of dumbbells—period, full stop. Sure, a barbell, weight plates, and a pull-up bar are great pickups as well, but they're not as beginner-friendly as one might be led to believe. Bench presses, pull-ups, and chin-ups are excellent for building muscle and strength in your back and chest, but they can be challenging for beginners.

The solution? "Grab a pair of dumbbells. Or even a single dumbbell," recommends Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., MH Fitness Director. The best dumbbells provide a versatile and accessible way to build strength, preparing you to slay multijoint lifts (like bench presses, rows, and deadlifts) while targeting smaller muscle groups (biceps, forearms) throughout the body. For novice lifters, incorporating the best dumbbell exercises into your routine helps build muscle and strength. That's especially true once you embrace heavier-weight dumbbell exercises such as RDLs and powerful presses and rows, Samuel explains.

In short, a set of dumbbells can vastly improve any home gym setup. They’re great for upper and lower body exercises, can help address muscular imbalances, and allow for gradual and predictable weight progression. The best part? They are not only more accessible and practical, but also more affordable than most other weightlifting tools.

When you’re in the market for new dumbbells, it’s easy to assume they’re all the same. While there's some truth to that, the devil is in the details. The best dumbbells feature a combination of durability, comfort, and versatility. Whether you prefer rubber or iron, adjustable or standard, keep an eye out for those that cater to your specific needs. Don't compromise on quality, as investing in the right set will pay off in the long run. Taking a moment to consider which set is the right fit for you is well worth the effort. Having extensively researched and tested numerous models over the years, we're here to guide you through a list of our all-time favorites. Here are our brutally honest picks of the best dumbbells to elevate your home workouts right now.

If you’re building the mother of all home gyms and money is no object, this comprehensive premium set of dumbbells from SMRTFT is our top recommendation. The Nüobell dumbbell set is crafted from near-bulletproof machined steel that’s built to outlast you. The included portable cradles make storage easy, and the compact design means the entire set takes up far less space than a set of typical fixed-weight dumbbells.

The adjustable design means you can use the same set of weights for every muscle group for a complete full body workout. Drop down to a little weight for bent-over flys, for example, or pile on the plates for more intense squats. It all adjusts seamlessly and easily with the built-in selector. Knurled handles make for safer lifting at any weight. "If you enjoy dropsets," says Samuel, "SMRTFT's bells shine, because no adjustable lets you swap weights as quickly."

Although there are thousands of fitness apps available, we also like the free app included with the SMRTFT dumbbells. It offers access to on-demand workouts with pro trainers, plus the ability to plan your own fitness journey, find nutrition tips, and get daily motivation. An all-around solid product that delivers on value in the long run.

Bowflex’s flagship dumbbell adjusts from 5 to 52.5 pounds, has a simple adjustment mechanism, and feels enough like a fixed set of dumbbells that most anyone will be pleased with them. And at under $500 for the pair, they’re a great deal, which is why they earned our “best value dumbbells” superlative in our guide to the best adjustable dumbbells.

My favorite aspect of these dumbbells is that they adjust in 2.5-pound increments up to 25 pounds (and then in 5-pound jumps from 25 to 50). It may not seem like a big deal, but five-pound jumps are pretty intense for single-joint exercises like dumbbell lateral raises.

The dial system is clear and easy to use, but it requires you to adjust a dial on either side of each dumbbell. It’s a pretty rudimentary adjustment system compared to the modern dumbbell market, and one that can lead to lop-sided dumbbells if you’re not paying close attention. Is it ideal? No. But is it a dealbreaker? Not a chance. It’s also worth noting that the 552s are mostly made of plastic, which gives them a cheap look and feel. That said, we consider these a budget buy, and plastic is significantly cheaper to build with than steel, so the plastic in this instance is more of a feature than a bug.

Due to their mostly plastic construction, we don’t recommend getting too rough with these dumbbells. I’ve been training with them for over six months and have had zero durability issues, but I wouldn’t feel comfortable dropping them after a set. Additionally, we find the design a bit wide and cumbersome for certain exercises, such as triceps extensions. "In my experience, these work best for chest-supported rows and overhead presses," says Samuel.

You’re not going to find many—if any—quality dumbbells with more weight than the 552s for a similar price. But, if you’re interested in buying heavier dumbbells, BowFlex offers the Results Series SelecTech 1090s, which boast a maximum load of 90 pounds per dumbbell.

Read More: Our Review of the Bowflex Results Series SelectTech 552 Dumbbells

It comes with the heftiest of price tags, but Hammer Strength’s line of 12-sided dumbbells is of the highest quality—a lifetime investment that’ll sting your pocket short-term but pay off for the long haul. These dumbbells are coated in durable urethane, feature a steel handle, and are trusted by pro athletes from commercial gyms to celebrities like Kane Brown.

You’ll need two things to make these dumbbells a reality in your home gym: money and space. The dumbbells are sold in sets (5-50, 55-75, 80-100, 105-125) or singles; both options will cost you thousands of dollars. And if you go with a set, you need the wall space (and racks, which cost even more) to house these dumbbells. Those are, as far as we’re concerned, the two most significant considerations for folks eyeing these dumbbells.

What I appreciate the most about these dumbbells is how familiar they feel in my hands—and that’s because they’re the same or close to the types of dumbbells commercial facilities use. The welded steel handle—which, I should add, is knurled to perfection—makes these the sturdiest dumbbells on our list. If you’re a serious strength athlete pushing over 80-pound dumbbells consistently, these are a solid investment. The 12-sided design prevents them from rolling, so you can use them for pushups and L-sits or, at the very least, you won’t have to chase them down after a hard set.

If the word "budget" isn’t in your vocabulary and you’re a fitness nut looking to build an S-tier home gym, Hammer Strength’s dumbbell sets are worth a serious look. Otherwise, most guys can reap the same benefits with a far more affordable set.

Sometimes simpler is better, especially for beginners and novices just starting out with lifting at home. This pair of straightforward dumbbells from CAP Barbell is about as barebones as it gets, and there's nothing wrong with that. The heads are crafted from rock-solid gray iron coated with odor-free rubber, and joined together with a cold-rolled steel chromed handle. They may not be adjustable, but it’s a tried-and-true design that’ll last for a really long time. We also like the medium depth knurling on the handles which allows for a surer grip while lifting.

The downside, says Samuel: Over time and very heavy usage, the rubber on these dumbbells may crack. And the standard (non-adjustable) design does mean that a full set takes up more floor space. But, if your home gym is starting to look a little cramped, consider going with a few pairs of dumbbells in varying weights to complement your existing setup without sacrificing too much room. They’re available in 5, 8, 10, 12, and 15-50-lb weights (in 5-lb increments).

REP Fitness is known for producing quality gym gear, and although it was late to the adjustable dumbbell party, the Quickdraw dumbbells are an innovative and hyper-affordable breath of fresh air in an increasingly crowded market space. The materials are durable, the adjustment system is whip-fast, and they offer plenty of options to scale up (albeit at a higher cost, of course).

First, let’s address the obvious elephant in the room. These dumbbells cost under $350, but that’s for a 30-pound pair, which is honestly going to be too light for most guys, especially for compound movements like rows and presses. You can change weights in 2.5- to 5-pound increments with the separate but included microplates or in 10-pound jumps using the built-in switches. REP also offers 40-, 50-, and 60-pound pairs at what we believe is still fair pricing, or you can purchase the add-on plates as your strength increases.

REP’s patented Lock-N-Load adjustment system is straightforward, allowing you to change weights simply by flipping a switch on each side of the dumbbell. We found the system incredibly fast and intuitive to use. Yes, you’ll need to place them back in their cradles, but it’s still a no-fuss adjustment that barely stalls our workouts.

Where these dumbbells excel—and where REP usually always excels—is with the build quality. REP says these are made with almost all-steel construction and supported by two powder-coated rods. My favorite feature is the steel handle that is fully covered in knurling; that’s the cross-hatch pattern you find in barbells that helps you grip the bar better. Knurled handles on adjustable dumbbells are exceedingly rare, especially at this price point.

These dumbbells arrive in two boxes and require minimal assembly upon arrival, which makes them an ultra-accessible choice for delivery and use at home.

PowerBlock’s EXP line might be the most clever design we’ve seen. Using the built-in polypropylene pin, you simply dial in the weight you want between 2.5-50 pounds per dumbbell (in varying increments). The unique design takes the place of a bulky and insanely heavy full set of standard dumbbells with a minimal footprint (just 12-in. x 6.5-in. per dumbbell). Plus, the pair stows easily with no storage tray or cradle required.

It’s great for apartment dwellers and anyone without the room for a lavish, 1,000-square-foot home gym setup. The powder-coated welded steel construction is also extremely durable and designed to protect against rust and corrosion.

We especially love that PowerBlock offers expansion kits for lifters who outgrow the 100-pound limit of this “entry-level” kit. Successive kits allow for up to 70- and 90-pound weight limits per dumbbell, respectively. This is a great option for newbie and mid-weight lifters who want to start out small and grow their strength over time.

The only other thing that might take getting used to is the square form factor. It doesn’t feel as natural to lift as traditional free weights, so it may not be for everyone.

Titan’s loadable handles are more akin to a barbell—where you slide on and secure weight plates to each side of the implement—than a traditional selectorized adjustable dumbbell. Titan’s loadable handles are made entirely of metal, feature knurling in the middle for superior grip, and rotate on bronze bushings. And for less than $150, they’re the most affordable “adjustable” dumbbells in our guide.

We put "adjustable" in quotes because, while these handles are an excellent value, there’s a catch: You need standard weight plates to load onto them. Now, if you’re rocking a complete home gym with a full set of plates and clamps to hold them in place, Titan’s handles are a great way to add dumbbell capability for a fraction of the cost of a full set of fixed dumbbells or a premium adjustable pair. Each handle can hold 400 pounds, so you’re never going to outgrow them strength-wise.

Loadable handles can feel clunky depending on the types of plates you load on them. For the best feel, stick with 2.5-, 5-, and 10-pound metal plates. If you go with bumper and/or heavier metal plates, the larger diameter will drastically throw off your range of motion on practically every exercise you try to perform.

As with any new home fitness gear, you should always consider your own training goals first. If you’re looking to supplement your existing powerlifting or bodybuilding training with accessory work, a set of adjus tables is best. If, however, you’re looking to do Olympic lifts, rubber hex dumbbells are the way to go.

How much available space do you have? If you’re a city dweller, live in a cramped apartment, or are shoehorning your home gym setup into the corner of a garage, consider an adjustable set of dumbbells. These take up far less space than a full (and massive) set that includes a rack and a bunch of fixed dumbbell weights that individually weigh between 10 and 100 pounds.

Here, it comes down to your available space and a bit of personal preference. In most cases, adjustable dumbbells are the way to go. They take up far less space and are often a little bit cheaper than standard, fixed weight alternatives. The downside: Even at lighter weights, adjustables are often larger than their fixed-weight counterparts, which can limit range of motion on certain movements.

Basically, does the dumbbell feel “good” or natural to you? Again, this comes down to personal preference, and might involve a trip to your local sporting goods store or gym equipment provider to compare a few models in person.

We’re talking about what your dumbbells are made of and how durable they are. We recommend rubber hex dumbbells for the vast majority of fitness types. They’re extremely durable, designed to take a beating, including being dropped, dragged around, and lord knows what else. Buy one decent set of hex rubber dumbbells, and there’s a good chance you won’t have to buy another set for a very long time, if ever.

Budget is important for just about every home gym builder. For many people, this might be the deciding factor. We recommend adjustable dumbbells for most fitness types, and they’re typically the most affordable. If, on the other hand, you have the space and extra money to burn, a dedicated set of rubber or iron hex dumbbells might be the better way to go.

As the Fitness and Commerce Editor at Men's Health, it's my job to test the latest and greatest gym equipment available, and that includes dumbbells. This was far from a solo effort though; I worked with MH contributor, Andrew Gutman, NASM-CPT, and leaned on the expertise of MH Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S.. I also worked with the larger MH team, as Brett Williams, NASM, and others put dozens of dumbbell models through the wringer. Samuel also utilized the top-performing dumbbells while training several of his clients.

Each dumbbell was rigorously tested in a variety of categories, including design, durability, functionality, and effectiveness. All dumbbells were tested with three types of exercises: Explosive exercises (like swings and cleans), multi-joint strength exercises (like bench presses and Romanian deadlifts), and accessory motions (like biceps curls and lateral raises). A minimum of 10 sets and 100 reps were performed at both comfortable and near-max weights for each motion. All dumbbells were also dropped from a basic bench to test baseline durability and were monitored for signs of rust over a three-month period.

We also consulted with both our MH Advisory Board and our Strength in Diversity trainers for deeper anecdotal and experiential thoughts on the best dumbbells. The list below represents our carefully considered picks for the best dumbbells to upgrade your home gym.

As we’re fond of saying, there’s no “best dumbbell material,” but rather what’s best for you. Dumbbells come in a handful of major construction types—each with their own strengths and weaknesses.

Traditional steel dumbbells usually lack a protective coating. That means that, while they’re incredibly strong, they’re also susceptible to rust and corrosion over time.

These are the classic dumbbells you’re probably used to seeing on TV and in old-school gyms around the world.

This is the material we recommend for just about everyone. Rubber is extremely strong, built to last for many years to come. Some models do keep that familiar rubber smell, however, which can be off-putting and hard to completely get rid of.

Urethane is a special type of rubber that’s even more durable than traditional rubber. The downside? That means it usually costs more.

We can’t think of any fitness type that would benefit from plastic dumbbells over any other material. They feel cheap (usually because they are) and just don’t hold up as well as rubber or metal alternatives.

So, why should you invest in a set of dumbbells? In short, they’re arguably the most versatile, best bang-for-your-buck addition to any home gym setup—all of which is why our own Ebenezer Samuel is a big fan of dumbbells. He’s previously shared at least 15 ways to smoke your back using dumbbells, including Dumbbell Pullovers, Elevated Plank Row Holds, and, most importantly, a wide variety of rows.

Our fitness team here at Men's Health created a program that delivers six epic dumbbell workouts.

The program, "The Only Six Dumbbell Workouts You'll Ever Need," provides more than just the half-dozen routines promised in the title. You'll learn the principles behind this type of training, including guidance on picking the right weight, form instructions, and even advice on nutrition to make sure you're fueling the right way while you take on the workouts.

For fitness, a little goes a long way, especially in your workouts. Short and fast doses can be the most optimal for your lifestyle, and that's where the best dumbbells come in handy. Life's too short for fussing with a ton of equipment during your workout window. Dumbbells get the job done.

#4776. Dutch startup Elysian says electric flight may be closer than you think

They day you get to book an all-electric flight may be closer than you think if Dutch startup Elysian Aircraft gets its way. Their new E9X commercial airliner promises flights that are a whole lot quieter, and at prices that are whole lot less dependent on dumb oil wars.

Aircraft account for more than 2% of global heating when CO₂ and other emissions are taken into account, with the share considerably higher in wealthy countries, according to data cited by climate campaign group Stay Grounded. Elysian Aircraft is keenly aware of the industry’s climate impact, and they believe their planned full-size electric airliner will be perfectly positioned to make a dramatic difference.

“By being able to transport 90 passengers for initially 800 kilometers and eventually 1,000 kilometers you can reduce emissions to zero, from half the world’s flights,” Elysian co-founder Daniel Jacobson told EuroNews. “That is a very large amount of flight activity in the world. And you reduce total emissions from aerospace by 20%.”

At the core of those ambitious emission-reduction goals is the Elysian E9X aircraft. Designed in collaboration with aerospace researchers at Delft University of Technology (TU Delft), the E9X packs its oversized wings with modular battery packs, sending power to six propellers driven by electric motors.

Specs on those haven’t been revealed, but the E9X is designed to carry up to 100 passengers up to 1,000 km (~620 miles) from where they started. Elysian says that’s enough range to handle nearly 50% of scheduled commercial passenger flights worldwide and potentially eliminate 20% of total in-flight emissions when the plane enters service in 2034.

That said, the E9X is far more than “just a concept,” and Elysian has completed its second conceptual design review and flown a scaled demonstrator in concert with Germany’s DLR aerospace research center, demonstrating how its unique battery packaging solutions address the challenges of integrating heavy battery packs into an aircraft’s wings (where fuel is traditionally stored).

It’s interesting to see all the comments that point out the difficulties and problems associated with the introduction of battery powered aircraft into the mainstream industry. What none of them address is the industry’s obsession with cutting their operating costs no matter what pain passengers and flight crews must endure. My bet is if the airlines can save money by converting to battery powered aircraft—there are NO obstacles that will stop them from doing it. Battery electric aircraft may reduce operating costs by thousands of dollars per flight. That alone tells me that they will be flying passengers as soon as possible.

The company is also working with airline partners KLM and Transavia to explore the operational and commercial requirements for putting electric airliners into service, with aircraft lessor TrueNoord investigating how the E9X could be financed and supported commercially.
